title: Who runs a mutual fund: sponsor, trustee, AMC, custodian
concept: A mutual fund is a trust. The sponsor sets it up, the trustees watch over it, and the asset management company (AMC) manages the money.
The custodian holds the securities, not the AMC. The registrar and transfer agent (RTA) keeps the unit records.
SEBI is the market regulator and writes the mutual fund rules. AMFI is the industry body that runs the ARN registration and the code of conduct.
Your money is invested in units of a scheme. It is not a deposit with the AMC, so the AMC's own finances do not hold your investment.
If an AMC shuts a scheme or changes it, the trustees and SEBI rules decide what unit holders are told and allowed to do.

client.quote: "What happens to my money if the AMC goes bust?"
client.context: Client worried about the fund house failing.

talk: "Your units are held in a trust, and the securities sit with a separate custodian. The AMC manages the money but does not own it. The fund can still lose value when markets fall, but a fund house failing is not the same as your money disappearing."
remember: SEBI regulates; AMFI runs the industry code.

qs.prompt: Who holds the securities a mutual fund buys?
qs.why: A separate custodian holds the securities. That separation protects unit holders if the AMC has trouble.

qs.prompt: A mutual fund is legally set up as:
qs.why: Mutual funds in India are trusts. The sponsor creates the trust, trustees oversee it and the AMC manages it.

qs.prompt: Which body runs the ARN registration for distributors?
qs.why: AMFI, the industry body, registers distributors and issues ARNs. SEBI sets the rules they follow.

title: Categories, riskometer and true-to-label investing
concept: SEBI sorts schemes into categories such as equity, debt, hybrid, solution-oriented and others, so that two funds with the same label behave alike.
Inside equity, categories like large cap, mid cap and small cap have minimum holdings in their segment. This stops a large cap fund drifting into small caps.
The riskometer shows a scheme's risk on a scale from low to very high. It is updated regularly based on what the fund actually holds.
The label tells you what the fund must do. It does not tell you how well it will do. Two funds in one category can differ a lot in return.
Compare a fund with others in its own category and benchmark. Comparing a small cap fund with a liquid fund tells you nothing.

client.quote: "This mid cap fund gave 28% and your large cap gave 14%. Why would I hold the large cap?"
client.context: Client comparing funds across categories.

talk: "They are built for different jobs and carry different risk. The mid cap can fall much harder. Let's compare each fund with the others in its own category, and match the risk to what you can stay invested through."

qs.prompt: Why does SEBI define fund categories?
options: So funds with the same label follow similar rules
qs.why: Categories make funds of one label comparable and stop style drift. They do not promise returns.

qs.prompt: The riskometer is best used to:
options: Judge how risky the scheme's holdings are
Compare a fund with a bank FD
qs.why: It shows the risk level of what the scheme holds. It says nothing about future returns.

qs.prompt: The fairest way to judge a mid cap fund is to compare it with:
options: Other mid cap funds and its benchmark
qs.why: Same category, same benchmark. Cross-category comparison mixes up risk and return.

title: Costs: expense ratio, loads and direct vs regular
concept: The total expense ratio (TER) is the yearly fee taken from the fund's assets. It is already reflected in the NAV, so you never see a separate bill.
A direct plan has no distributor commission, so its TER is lower than the regular plan of the same scheme. The portfolio is the same.
An exit load is a fee for leaving early, charged on the amount redeemed within a stated period. Many equity funds have one for a year or less. Check the scheme document.
A small difference in TER compounds. A 1% gap over 20 years can shrink the final amount by a meaningful slice.
A regular plan pays for advice and service. The honest question is whether the advice is worth what it costs.

client.quote: "Why should I pay more through you when direct plans are cheaper?"
client.context: Client who has read about direct plans.

talk: "The direct plan is cheaper and that is a real saving. What you get from us is the plan, the review, and someone who talks you out of selling at the bottom. Let's look at the numbers and decide whether that is worth the difference to you."

qs.prompt: Where does a fund's expense ratio show up?
options: It is already deducted from the NAV
qs.why: TER is charged to the scheme and reflected in the NAV every day.

qs.prompt: Direct and regular plans of the same scheme differ in:
qs.why: The portfolio is identical. Regular carries a commission, so its TER is higher.

qs.prompt: An exit load is charged when you:
qs.why: Exit load applies to redemptions made within the period in the scheme document.

title: KYC, nomination and a clean paper trail
concept: KYC (know your customer) is required to invest. It is a one-time process with identity and address proof, and is valid across fund houses once done.
Nomination lets the investor name who receives the units. Not nominating, or opting out, can make claims slow and painful for the family.
Joint holding with 'either or survivor' lets one holder operate the folio. Choose the mode deliberately.
Keep the folio's mobile and email current. Account statements and alerts go there, and changes are verified through them.
A distributor must hold a valid ARN and show the ARN and EUIN on the application. Always check that it is correct.

client.quote: "Do I really need to fill the nominee? I will do it later."
client.context: Client skipping nomination on the form.

talk: "Please do it now, it takes a minute. If something happens, the nominee gets the units without a long legal process. You can change it any time."

qs.prompt: What does nomination do?
options: Names who receives the units on the holder's death
qs.why: A nominee receives the units, which makes the family's claim simpler.

qs.prompt: A distributor's application should always show:
qs.why: The ARN identifies the registered distributor.

qs.prompt: Why keep the mobile and email in a folio up to date?
options: It is needed to switch plans
qs.why: Account statements, OTPs and alerts are sent to the registered contact details.

title: What you may and may not say: advertising and mis-selling
concept: Mutual fund advertising must carry the standard statement: mutual fund investments are subject to market risks; read all scheme related documents carefully.
Past performance can be shown only within the rules, and always with the line that it may or may not be sustained in future.
You must not promise or imply a return, guarantee capital, or call a market-linked scheme 'safe'.
Mis-selling includes pushing a product for the commission rather than the client's need, hiding costs, or recommending unsuitable risk.
Suitability comes first. Record the client's goal, horizon and risk comfort before you recommend.

client.quote: "Can you promise me at least 12% a year?"
client.context: Client asking for a guarantee.

talk: "I can't promise that and neither can anyone honest. Over long periods equity has done well, but the path is uneven. Let's build a plan that works even if returns are lower, and review it every year."

qs.prompt: Which statement is a promise you must not make?
options: "This fund will give you 12% every year."
qs.why: Promising a return in a market-linked product is mis-selling.

qs.prompt: Mis-selling includes:
options: Recommending a product mainly for commission
qs.why: Recommending for commission instead of suitability is mis-selling.

qs.prompt: Showing past returns needs which line?
options: That past performance may or may not be sustained
A guarantee of the same return
qs.why: Past performance cannot be presented as a promise of future results.

title: When things go wrong: grievances and investor protection
concept: Start with the fund house's investor service team, and keep the reference number. Most issues end here.
If the reply is late or unsatisfactory, escalate through SEBI's complaint platform, SCORES. Complaints are tracked against timelines.
SEBI's online dispute resolution (ODR) route is available once internal escalation does not work.
Unclaimed amounts sit with the fund house and can be claimed with proof. Keep KYC and bank details current.
Good records protect everyone: application copies, statements, and notes of what was discussed with the client.

client.quote: "My redemption has not arrived in a week. Who do I complain to?"
client.context: Client stuck on a delayed payout.

talk: "First, write to the fund house and note the reference. If they don't resolve it in the stated time, we escalate on SEBI's SCORES platform. I'll help you with the paperwork."

qs.prompt: Where should a complaint start?
options: With the fund house's investor service team
qs.why: Most problems are solved at the first level. Keep the reference.

qs.prompt: SEBI's online platform for complaints is:
qs.why: SCORES lets investors lodge and track complaints against listed entities and intermediaries.

qs.prompt: Why keep copies of applications and statements?
options: They are the proof if there is a dispute
qs.why: Records settle disputes quickly and protect both client and advisor.

title: Large, mid and small: how the market-cap ladder works
concept: AMFI ranks listed companies by market capitalisation. The top 100 are large caps, ranks 101 to 250 are mid caps, and 251 onward are small caps.
Large caps are bigger, more liquid and usually steadier. Small caps can grow faster but fall harder and are harder to sell in a crash.
A large cap fund must keep at least 80% in large caps. Mid cap and small cap funds must keep at least 65% in their own segment.
Companies move between buckets as prices change, so a fund's mix of stocks changes without the manager doing anything.
Long-term returns tend to rise with risk across the ladder, but with long flat or negative stretches. Match the bucket to the client's horizon.

client.quote: "Small caps gave the highest return. Put everything there."
client.context: Client chasing last year's winner.

talk: "Small caps have the highest ceiling and the deepest falls. Let's keep them as one part of the portfolio, sized so a bad year doesn't push you to sell."

qs.prompt: Under AMFI's list, mid caps are companies ranked:
qs.why: Large = 1-100, mid = 101-250, small = 251 onward.

qs.prompt: A large cap fund must hold at least what share in large caps?
qs.why: SEBI's categorisation requires a minimum of 80% in large caps.

qs.prompt: Why can a fund's portfolio drift between buckets without trades?
options: Company market caps change and ranks move
qs.why: Rankings follow market value, so stocks cross the line as prices move.

title: Flexi cap, multi cap and focused funds
concept: A multi cap fund must keep at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps. The manager chooses the rest.
A flexi cap fund can invest in any mix of market caps with no minimum for each, so the manager has the most freedom.
A focused fund holds at most 30 stocks. High conviction means that one wrong stock hurts more.
Flexi cap suits a client who wants one core equity fund and trusts the manager to shift between segments.
Check what the fund actually holds. The label sets the range, the factsheet shows the real mix.

client.quote: "I want just one equity fund. Which type?"
client.context: Client with a single-fund mindset.

talk: "A flexi cap is a reasonable one-fund core because the manager can move between large, mid and small caps. We'll check what it really holds every year, and I'll tell you if it drifts from your risk comfort."

qs.prompt: A multi cap fund must hold at least how much in each of large, mid and small caps?
qs.why: SEBI requires a minimum 25% in each segment.

qs.prompt: A focused fund holds at most:
qs.why: SEBI caps focused funds at 30 stocks.

qs.prompt: The main risk of a focused fund is:
options: It must be sold in a year
Each stock has a larger effect on returns
qs.why: With few stocks, one bad pick moves the whole fund.

title: ELSS: the tax-saving equity fund
concept: An ELSS (equity linked savings scheme) is an equity fund with a three-year lock-in. It qualifies for the section 80C deduction under the old tax regime.
The lock-in is the shortest among 80C options. Each SIP instalment is locked for three years from its own date.
ELSS must invest at least 80% in equity, so it carries full equity risk. The tax benefit does not reduce market risk.
Under the new tax regime, 80C is not available. For such clients ELSS is just an equity fund with a lock-in.
Pick ELSS for the fund quality, not only the tax. Staying invested after the lock-in is usually the better choice.

client.quote: "I need to save tax before March. Which ELSS should I buy?"
client.context: Client rushing at year-end.

talk: "First, are you on the old regime? If yes, ELSS can help with 80C. Pick it for the fund, not just the deduction, and consider an SIP across the year instead of one lump sum in March."

qs.prompt: The lock-in period of an ELSS is:
qs.why: ELSS has a three-year lock-in, counted for each purchase.

qs.prompt: Does the ELSS deduction work under the new tax regime?
qs.why: 80C deductions are an old-regime benefit.

qs.prompt: An ELSS SIP of 12 monthly instalments has:
options: One lock-in from the first date
A lock-in only on the last instalment
Each instalment locked for 3 years from its date
qs.why: Every instalment has its own three-year lock-in.

title: Sectoral and thematic funds: narrow bets
concept: A sectoral fund invests at least 80% in one sector, such as banking or pharma. A thematic fund follows a wider idea, such as consumption or manufacturing.
Both are concentrated. When the theme is in favour, returns can be big. When it is out of favour, falls are deep and long.
They are usually satellite holdings, not the core of a portfolio.
Beware of buying a theme after it has already run. NFOs often arrive near the top of a theme.
Size them small, and agree beforehand when you will review or exit.

client.quote: "Defence stocks are flying. Put half my money there."
client.context: Client chasing a hot theme.

talk: "The story is real, but so is the risk of buying after a big run. Let's keep it to a small slice of the portfolio and agree when we'll review it."

qs.prompt: A sectoral fund must hold at least what share in its sector?
qs.why: Sectoral funds invest a minimum of 80% in their chosen sector.

qs.prompt: Sectoral and thematic funds are usually best as:
qs.why: Their concentration makes them unsuitable as a sole core holding.

qs.prompt: The danger of buying a theme after a big rally is:
options: You may buy near a peak and face a long fall
qs.why: Strong past performance often reflects prices already high.

title: Value, contra and dividend yield: style funds
concept: A value fund buys stocks that look cheap compared with earnings or assets. A contra fund bets against the crowd on out-of-favour stocks.
Each of these must hold at least 65% in equity. A fund can follow value or contra, but not both labels.
Value can lag for years when growth stocks lead, then catch up. Patience is the price of the style.
A dividend yield fund holds high-dividend stocks. The dividend does not make it less risky.
A client who needs steady results every year may be unhappy with a style that goes in and out of favour.

client.quote: "The value fund has trailed the market for three years. Should I sell?"
client.context: Client losing patience with a style.

talk: "Value styles do go through long dry spells, and that is exactly when most people leave. Let's check whether the fund is doing what it promised, not whether it is winning this year."
remember: Dividend yield is not low risk.

qs.prompt: A value fund tends to buy:
options: Stocks that look cheap against fundamentals
qs.why: Value investing targets stocks priced low compared with earnings or assets.

qs.prompt: A style fund that trails for three years should be judged on:
options: Whether it follows its stated style and process
qs.why: Judge the fund on its approach and long-term record, not one stretch.

qs.prompt: A dividend yield fund is:
options: Still an equity fund with market risk
qs.why: High-dividend stocks can still fall.

title: Choosing an equity fund: a simple, honest method
concept: Start with the goal and horizon, then pick the category. Only then compare funds.
Compare funds in the same category over several rolling periods, not a single calendar year.
Look at consistency, downside in bad years, portfolio concentration, and cost, not just the headline return.
Check the fund's age, the manager's tenure and the fund size. Very large size can hurt mid and small cap funds.
Hold a small number of funds. Many overlapping funds add paperwork, not diversification.

client.quote: "Here are 12 funds my colleague suggested. Can I buy all of them?"
client.context: Client over-diversifying.

talk: "Twelve funds will likely hold many of the same stocks. Let's pick a few that do different jobs, and check overlap before buying."

qs.prompt: What should you decide first when picking an equity fund?
qs.why: Goal and horizon decide the category and the risk.

qs.prompt: Why check overlap between funds?
options: Funds may hold the same stocks, so diversification is less than it looks
qs.why: Overlap shows how much of the portfolio is duplicated.

qs.prompt: A better way to read fund performance than a single year is:
options: Rolling returns across many start dates
qs.why: Rolling returns show how consistent a fund has been through cycles.

title: The hybrid family at a glance
concept: Hybrid funds mix equity and debt, and some also hold gold or other assets. The category tells you the rough mix.
Aggressive hybrid: 65% to 80% equity, the rest debt. Conservative hybrid: 10% to 25% equity, the rest mostly debt.
Balanced advantage (dynamic asset allocation) changes its equity share with market valuations. Equity savings holds equity, arbitrage and debt.
Arbitrage funds hold hedged equity and are taxed like equity funds. They behave like low-risk debt funds with stable returns.
Multi asset funds must hold at least three asset classes, with at least 10% in each.

client.quote: "I want something between FD and equity. What are my options?"
client.context: Cautious investor stepping into markets.

talk: "There are a few middle paths. A conservative hybrid has a little equity, a balanced advantage fund moves its equity share with valuations, and an aggressive hybrid is mostly equity. Let's match one to how much fall you can handle."

qs.prompt: An aggressive hybrid fund holds how much in equity?
qs.why: The category range is 65% to 80% equity.

qs.prompt: A balanced advantage fund:
options: Changes equity exposure with market valuations
qs.why: Dynamic asset allocation shifts equity share through cycles.

qs.prompt: A multi asset fund must hold:
options: At least 10% in each of three or more asset classes
qs.why: SEBI requires three asset classes with a minimum of 10% each.

title: How arbitrage funds work
concept: The fund buys a stock in the cash market and sells the same stock in the futures market at a higher price. The gap between them is locked in as profit.
Because the position is hedged, the fund barely moves with the stock market. Returns track short-term interest rates.
At least 65% is in equity-related instruments, so the fund is taxed as an equity fund. This is the main attraction for investors in high tax slabs.
Returns can dip when the futures premium narrows, such as when markets are weak and there is less demand for leverage.
It is a short-term parking option, not a growth engine.

client.quote: "Can I park ₹20 lakh for a year in something safer than equity but better taxed than an FD?"
client.context: High-bracket client with idle cash.

talk: "An arbitrage fund can fit. It's hedged, so it moves little with markets, and it is taxed as equity. Returns stay near short-term rates, so expect FD-like numbers, not equity growth."

qs.prompt: An arbitrage fund earns by:
options: Capturing the gap between cash and futures prices
qs.why: It buys in cash and sells futures to lock in the spread.

qs.prompt: Arbitrage funds are taxed as:
qs.why: They hold at least 65% in equity-related instruments, so equity tax rules apply.

qs.prompt: What do arbitrage fund returns usually resemble?
qs.why: The hedged spread tends to track short-term rates.

title: Balanced advantage funds: how the dial turns
concept: A balanced advantage fund moves its net equity between low and high levels. When markets look expensive it reduces equity, and when they look cheap it increases it.
It uses a model, often based on valuations such as price to earnings or price to book, to set the equity level.
Hedging with futures keeps the tax status equity-like while the net equity level changes.
It can reduce the pain in a fall, but it can also lag in a strong rally because it holds back at high valuations.
Compare funds by their model, how often it changes, and how it behaved in 2020 and other stress periods.

client.quote: "Does this fund protect me when markets fall?"
client.context: Client wants downside protection.

talk: "It tries to reduce risk when valuations are high, so falls are often smaller than in a pure equity fund. It doesn't remove losses, and in strong rallies it can trail."

qs.prompt: A balanced advantage fund lowers equity when:
qs.why: Models reduce equity as markets get pricey.

qs.prompt: A downside of a balanced advantage fund is:
options: It can trail in strong rallies
qs.why: Holding back at high valuations can mean missing part of a rally.

qs.prompt: To compare balanced advantage funds, look at:
options: The model and its behaviour in past falls
qs.why: The allocation model drives outcomes. Check its record in stress periods.

title: Equity savings and conservative hybrids
concept: An equity savings fund holds equity, arbitrage and debt. Net equity is usually in a modest range, and the fund is taxed as an equity fund if 65% is in equity and arbitrage together.
A conservative hybrid holds mostly debt with a small slice of equity. Its gains are generally taxed at slab rate, like a debt fund.
These suit people who want a bit of equity upside with lower swings, such as retirees or first-time investors.
The debt part carries credit and interest rate risk. Check its quality.
Returns will be modest. Expect steady, not spectacular.

client.quote: "My father is 70 and wants better than an FD but cannot take big falls."
client.context: Retiree seeking gentle growth.

talk: "A conservative hybrid or equity savings fund could suit. They hold some equity for growth with a larger debt or arbitrage base. Expect moderate returns and small falls, not zero."

qs.prompt: An equity savings fund holds:
qs.why: It blends the three to dampen swings.

qs.prompt: A conservative hybrid is mainly:
options: Equity with a small debt portion
Debt with a small equity portion
qs.why: The category keeps 10% to 25% in equity.

qs.prompt: Who might suit a conservative hybrid?
options: A retiree wanting modest growth with small falls
qs.why: Lower volatility fits those who dislike big falls.

title: Taxing hybrids: the 65% line
concept: A fund with at least 65% in equity-related instruments is taxed as an equity fund. Gains over one year are long-term.
Equity LTCG over the annual exemption is taxed at 12.5%, and short-term gains at 20% (confirm current rates with a tax advisor).

Funds with 35% to 65% in equity sit in between: gains held over 24 months are long-term at 12.5%, otherwise slab rate. Funds with mostly debt (equity below 35%) are generally taxed at slab rate whatever the holding period.
Arbitrage and equity savings funds use the 65% line, which is why they exist in their tax-efficient form.
Always check the fund's tax status, not just its name.

client.quote: "Will I pay tax like an FD on this hybrid fund?"
client.context: Client asking about tax.

talk: "It depends on the equity share. At 65% or more, it's taxed like an equity fund. Below that, the rules differ and many such funds are taxed at your slab rate. Please confirm with your CA for your own situation."
remember: Check the fund, not the name.

qs.prompt: A hybrid fund is taxed as equity when equity-related holdings are at least:
qs.why: The 65% threshold decides equity treatment.

qs.prompt: A hybrid fund with only 20% in equity and the rest in debt is generally taxed:
options: At slab rate on gains, whatever the holding period
qs.why: With mostly debt holdings, gains are generally taxed at the investor's slab rate. Confirm with a tax advisor.

qs.prompt: To know a fund's tax treatment you should check:
options: Its actual asset mix and category
qs.why: Tax follows holdings, not the name.

title: Matching a hybrid to the client
concept: Start with the shortfall the client can handle, then pick the hybrid whose worst falls fit it.
For a first-time investor, a balanced advantage or aggressive hybrid can be an easy entry that reduces regret.
For idle cash with a year or less, arbitrage may fit. For more than three years, plain equity or hybrid funds can suit.
Avoid stacking several hybrids that hold the same assets.
Review once a year and rebalance the whole portfolio, not each fund.

client.quote: "I'm nervous about equity. Where do I begin?"
client.context: First-time investor.

talk: "We'll start with a hybrid that holds some equity but cushions the falls, and add a pure equity fund once you are comfortable. We'll review every year."
remember: Fit the fall, not the return.

qs.prompt: For a nervous first-time investor, a sensible start is:
options: A hybrid with a cushioned equity share
qs.why: Hybrid funds ease people into equity.

qs.prompt: Holding many hybrids with similar assets mainly gives:
qs.why: Similar portfolios duplicate the same exposure.

qs.prompt: How often should a portfolio be reviewed at minimum?
qs.why: An annual review is a sensible minimum.

title: SIP myths and what rupee-cost averaging really does
concept: An SIP invests a fixed amount at regular dates. When the NAV is low you get more units, when it is high you get fewer, so your average cost per unit sits below the average price.
This lowers the stress of timing. It does not guarantee a profit or protect against a long fall.
SIP returns are measured with XIRR, since each instalment has a different holding period.
An SIP works best over long periods, through at least one full market cycle.
Stopping an SIP in a fall is the most common way to lose the benefit.

client.quote: "Markets are down 15%. Should I pause my SIP?"
client.context: Client scared by a fall.

talk: "A fall is when the same amount buys more units. Pausing means you stop buying at lower prices. If your goal is still far away, staying the course is usually the plan."

qs.prompt: In an SIP, a lower NAV means:
options: You get more units for the same amount
qs.why: Fixed money buys more units when prices are low.

qs.prompt: Which measure fits SIP returns best?
qs.why: XIRR accounts for the different dates of each instalment.

qs.prompt: SIPs cannot:
qs.why: No investment method removes market risk.

title: Step-up SIPs: letting investing grow with income
concept: A step-up SIP raises the instalment by a set amount or percentage each year, such as 10%.
Because income usually rises over time, a step-up lets the investment keep pace without effort.
The final corpus can be far larger than a flat SIP, even with a small yearly step.
Set the step to something the client can sustain. A step that is too high can cause missed instalments.
Reviewing the step each year, along with the goal, keeps the plan honest.

client.quote: "I can only invest ₹10,000 now, but my salary will grow."
client.context: Young earner with a rising income.

talk: "Start at ₹10,000 and raise it 10% each year. You'll hardly feel the change, and the corpus at the end can be much larger than a flat SIP."

qs.prompt: A step-up SIP:
options: Raises the instalment on a schedule
qs.why: The instalment increases by a fixed amount or percentage.

qs.prompt: The main benefit of a step-up is:
options: The investment keeps pace with growing income
qs.why: Raising contributions matches rising income.

qs.prompt: A risk of setting a step-up too high is:
options: Missed instalments when cash flow is tight
qs.why: A step you cannot sustain can lead to a stopped SIP.

title: Lump sum, SIP or STP: choosing how to enter
concept: A lump sum puts all the money in at once. It does well if markets rise soon after, and badly if they fall.
An SIP spreads new savings over time. It suits regular income.
An STP (systematic transfer plan) moves a lump sum from a safe fund, often liquid or short duration, to an equity fund in instalments.
No method wins every time. The best one is the one the client can stick with.
STP gives a client with a large lump sum comfort. The money waiting in debt keeps earning something.

client.quote: "I got ₹30 lakh from a property sale. Invest it all today?"
client.context: Client with a large lump sum.

talk: "We can park it in a liquid fund and move it into equity over, say, six to twelve months through an STP. You earn something on the waiting money, and you won't regret a single day's entry."
remember: STP: debt to equity in steps.
Best method is the one they follow.

qs.prompt: An STP moves money:
options: From one scheme to another in instalments
From a bank to a stock
qs.why: STP transfers units from a source fund into a target fund over time.

qs.prompt: Who benefits most from an STP?
options: Someone with a large lump sum
qs.why: STP smooths entry for a lump sum.

qs.prompt: The best way to invest is:
options: The one the client can stay with
qs.why: Behaviour matters more than the exact method.

title: SWP: turning a corpus into an income
concept: A systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) redeems a fixed amount from a fund every month, quarter or year.
Each withdrawal is part gain and part capital, so only the gain portion is taxed.
The fund keeps growing while you withdraw, so a modest rate can last a long time.
A high withdrawal rate in a falling market eats the corpus fast. This is sequence risk.
Keep one to two years of withdrawals in a lower-risk fund so you are never forced to sell equity in a fall.

client.quote: "Can I take ₹50,000 a month from my ₹1 crore corpus?"
client.context: Retiree planning income.

talk: "That's 6% a year. It may work, but if markets fall early it could run down quickly. A safer plan keeps two years of withdrawals in a steady fund and the rest invested for growth."

qs.prompt: In an SWP, what part of each withdrawal is taxed?
qs.why: Each redemption is part capital and part gain.

qs.prompt: Sequence risk means:
options: Early falls while withdrawing can drain the corpus
qs.why: Poor returns early in withdrawal do lasting damage.

qs.prompt: A sensible protection for an SWP is:
options: Holding one to two years of withdrawals in a steadier fund
qs.why: A buffer avoids selling equity at the bottom.

title: Goals first: from time horizon to asset mix
concept: Write down the goal, the amount needed in future rupees, and the date. Inflation raises the target.
Goals under three years usually belong in low-risk funds. Goals over seven years can hold more equity.
The shorter the horizon, the less you can afford a fall near the end. Shift to safer funds as the date nears.
Keep a separate fund or folio for each goal so progress is easy to see.
Review the goal each year. A change in income or cost should change the plan.

client.quote: "I want ₹50 lakh for my daughter's college in 12 years."
client.context: Parent with a clear goal.

talk: "We should adjust ₹50 lakh for inflation first, then work out the monthly amount. Over 12 years you can hold mostly equity for the first part, then move into safer funds over the last three years."

qs.prompt: For a goal two years away, funds are usually chosen from:
qs.why: Short horizons cannot absorb equity falls.

qs.prompt: Why adjust a goal for inflation?
options: Future costs are higher than today's
qs.why: The money needed will be larger in future rupees.

qs.prompt: What should happen to a goal portfolio as the date nears?
qs.why: Protect what has been gained as the date approaches.

title: SIP discipline: pauses, bounces and restarts
concept: An SIP is paid through a bank mandate. If the account lacks money on the date, the instalment bounces and the bank may charge a fee.
Three missed instalments in a row can cancel the SIP in many schemes, depending on the rules.

title: What passive investing really is
concept: A passive fund copies an index instead of trying to beat it. If the index holds 50 stocks in certain weights, the fund holds the same.
Costs are lower because there is no research team picking stocks.
The fund's return will be close to the index return, minus costs and tracking error.
Passive does not mean safe. An index fund falls when its index falls.

An ETF trades on the stock exchange all day and needs a demat account. You pay the market price, which can differ slightly from NAV.
ETFs have a small bid-ask spread when you trade, and low liquidity can make it wider.
Index funds suit SIP investors. ETFs suit people who trade with a demat and want intraday prices.

title: Tracking error and tracking difference
concept: Tracking difference is the gap between the fund's return and the index return over a period. It is mostly the expense ratio plus small frictions.
Tracking error is how much that gap wiggles from day to day. A low number means the fund follows its index closely.
A fund with a low expense ratio can still have poor tracking if it is badly managed.
Compare funds on the same index using tracking difference over one to three years.
Cash drag, delays in rebalancing and dividends can add to the gap.

title: Loss aversion: why a fall hurts twice as much

title: Shares, exchanges and who is in charge
concept: Before any trade, know what you are buying, where it trades and who keeps the market honest.

Share. A share is a unit of ownership in a company. A shareholder owns a small part of the business and shares in its profits and risks. For example: asha buys 10 units of a listed company and now owns a tiny slice of its business.

Stock exchange. A stock exchange is a regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers trade listed shares at transparent prices. India’s main exchanges are NSE and BSE. For example: buy and sell orders from thousands of investors are matched on a regulated electronic platform.

SEBI. SEBI is India’s securities market regulator. It protects investors, registers intermediaries and writes the rules for exchanges and brokers. For example: a broker is found misusing client funds and the market regulator steps in to penalise it.

Stockbroker. A stockbroker is a registered intermediary who places your buy and sell orders on the exchange and charges brokerage for the service. For example: ravi uses a registered app-based intermediary to place orders on the exchange for a small fee on each trade.

talk: “A share is a small piece of ownership in a real business. You trade it on a regulated exchange through a registered broker, and SEBI sets the rules. Nobody guarantees the price, but the system is built to be fair and transparent.”
remember: A share is ownership, not a loan.
Exchanges match buyers and sellers; SEBI regulates.

title: Accounts and order types
concept: Two accounts and a handful of order types are all you need to place a trade safely.

Demat account. A demat account holds your shares in electronic form, like a bank account holds money. The depositories NSDL and CDSL keep the records. For example: meena’s purchased shares are stored electronically in her name, with no paper certificates.

Trading account. A trading account is the account through which you place buy and sell orders. It connects your bank account and your demat account. For example: kabir logs in to place a buy order that debits his bank and delivers shares to his locker.

Limit order. A limit order buys or sells only at your chosen price or better. It may not execute if the market never reaches that price. For example: priya wants to buy at ₹500 or lower and will wait rather than pay ₹510.

Stop-loss order. A stop-loss order triggers a sale when the price falls to a level you set, to cap the loss on a position. In a fast fall it may fill below that level. For example: nikhil bought at ₹200 and sets an instruction to sell if the price drops to ₹180.

remember: Limit orders control price, not certainty.

title: How trades settle and prices move
concept: Prices change every second, but the rules for settlement, spreads and limits are fixed.

T+1 settlement. India settles most share trades one working day after the trade: shares and money change hands on the next working day. For example: shares bought on Monday are credited to the buyer’s demat account on Tuesday.

Bid-ask spread. The bid is the highest price a buyer offers and the ask is the lowest price a seller wants. The gap between them is a hidden cost of trading. For example: a share shows ₹100.00 for sellers to hit and ₹100.40 for buyers to pay at the same moment.

Price band. A price band limits how far a share can rise or fall in one day. When it is hit, trading in that share is halted or restricted for the day. For example: a stock reaches its daily upper limit and no buyer can push it higher that day.

Market capitalisation. Market capitalisation is the share price multiplied by the number of shares issued. It is the market’s value of the whole company. For example: a company has 100 crore shares trading at ₹50 each, valuing the business at ₹5,000 crore.

client.context: A client new to settlement timings.

talk: “Trades settle the next working day, called T+1. The shares and the money change hands then. A price band also limits how far a stock can move in a day, so extreme swings are contained.”
remember: The bid-ask spread is a cost.

title: IPOs and corporate actions
concept: Companies raise money, pay profits and reshape their shares. Know what each action does to you.

IPO. An initial public offering is when a company sells shares to the public for the first time to raise money, and then lists on an exchange. For example: a private company invites ordinary investors to apply for its first-ever shares before it lists.

Dividend. A dividend is a share of profit a company pays to shareholders, usually per share. The board decides it and it is not guaranteed. For example: a company pays ₹5 per share out of its profits to everyone on its register.

Stock split. A stock split divides each share into more shares at a lower price. The number of shares rises but the total value you own is unchanged. For example: a ₹1,000 share becomes two ₹500 shares and an investor’s 10 shares become 20.

Bonus issue. A bonus issue gives existing shareholders extra shares free, out of the company’s reserves. The price adjusts down, so total value stays about the same. For example: holders receive one free share for every two they own, and the price falls to reflect it.

title: Intraday, delivery and risk
concept: How long you hold, and how widely you spread your money, shapes your risk more than any single pick.
Delivery trade. In a delivery trade you take the shares into your demat account and can hold them for as long as you like. For example: sanjay buys shares on Monday and keeps them for five years.

Intraday trade. An intraday trade is opened and closed on the same day, so no shares are delivered. Profit or loss is the difference in price. For example: zara buys at 10 am and sells at 2 pm the same day and never takes delivery.

Nifty 50. The Nifty 50 is an index of 50 large companies listed on the NSE. It tracks the market’s direction but cannot be bought directly. For example: news says the main NSE benchmark of 50 large companies rose 1% today.

Diversification. Diversification spreads money across many shares, sectors or assets so that one failure does not sink the whole portfolio. For example: a client holds twelve companies across banking, IT, pharma and consumer goods rather than just one.

title: Earnings and the three statements
concept: Every company reports three statements. Together they show profit, position and cash.

Profit and loss statement. The profit and loss statement shows a company’s revenue, costs and profit over a period such as a quarter or a year. For example: an analyst opens the page showing sales, expenses and profit for the last quarter.

Balance sheet. The balance sheet is a snapshot on one date of what a company owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owners’ stake (equity). For example: an analyst checks what the company owns and owes as of 31 March.

Cash flow statement. The cash flow statement shows actual cash moving in and out through operations, investing and financing. For example: a profitable company is found to have collected very little cash from customers this year.

Earnings per share (EPS). Earnings per share is net profit divided by the number of shares. It shows how much profit each share earns. For example: a company earns ₹100 crore profit with 10 crore shares outstanding, so each share earns ₹10.

title: Valuation ratios
concept: Ratios compare price with earnings, assets and growth to judge whether a share looks expensive or cheap.

Price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. The P/E ratio is the share price divided by earnings per share. It shows how much investors pay for each rupee of earnings. For example: a share trades at ₹300 and earns ₹15 per share, so investors pay 20 times earnings.

Price-to-book (P/B) ratio. The P/B ratio compares the share price with book value per share, the net worth of the company divided by shares. It is often used for banks. For example: a lender trades at twice the net asset value per share on its books.

PEG ratio. The PEG ratio divides the P/E by the expected earnings growth rate, to judge whether a high P/E is justified by growth. For example: two companies have the same P/E, but one is expected to grow earnings twice as fast.

Dividend yield. Dividend yield is the annual dividend per share divided by the share price, shown as a percentage. It is the cash return before any price change. For example: a share priced at ₹200 pays ₹6 a year, so the cash return is 3%.

talk: “A low ratio can mean cheap, or it can mean the market sees trouble ahead. Compare with the company’s own history, its growth and its industry before deciding.”

title: Profitability and returns
concept: Good businesses earn high returns on the money they use, year after year.

Return on equity (ROE). Return on equity is net profit divided by shareholders’ equity. It shows how well a company turns owners’ money into profit. For example: a company earns ₹20 crore profit on ₹100 crore of owners’ funds each year.

Return on capital employed (ROCE). ROCE is operating profit divided by all capital used, both equity and debt. It shows how efficiently the whole business uses money. For example: an analyst compares operating profit with the total of owners’ funds and borrowings.

Operating margin. Operating margin is operating profit as a percentage of revenue. It shows how much profit is left from each rupee of sales before interest and tax. For example: a firm keeps ₹18 of operating profit from every ₹100 of sales.

Net profit margin. Net profit margin is net profit as a percentage of revenue. It shows how much of each rupee of sales finally becomes profit after all costs and taxes. For example: after every cost and tax, a company keeps ₹9 from each ₹100 of sales.

client.quote: “How do I tell a good business from a lucky one?”
client.context: A client who wants to pick stocks himself.

talk: “Look for businesses that earn high returns on the capital they use, over many years, without piling on debt. That consistency is rarer than a single great year.”

title: Debt, safety and ownership
concept: Borrowing multiplies both gains and troubles. Ownership patterns show who is confident in the business.

Debt-to-equity ratio. The debt-to-equity ratio compares a company’s borrowings with owners’ equity. A higher number means more reliance on borrowed money. For example: a firm has ₹200 crore of loans against ₹100 crore of owners’ funds.

Interest coverage ratio. Interest coverage is operating profit divided by interest expense. It shows how comfortably a company can pay its interest bills. For example: a company’s operating profit is six times its yearly interest cost.

Promoter holding. Promoter holding is the percentage of a company owned by its founders or controlling group. Stable, high holding shows commitment, but quality still matters. For example: a founding family owns 60% of the company’s shares.

Pledged shares. Pledged shares are promoter shares put up as security for a loan. If the price falls, lenders can sell them, which can hit the share price. For example: promoters borrowed against their own shares and lenders may sell if the price drops.

title: Cash, growth and quality
concept: Cash generation, steady growth and clean accounting separate durable businesses from stories.

Free cash flow. Free cash flow is cash from operations minus the money spent to maintain and grow the business. It is what is truly left for owners and lenders. For example: after paying for machines and expansion, a company still has ₹50 crore of cash left over.

Revenue growth. Revenue growth is the rate at which a company’s sales increase over time. Steady growth over many years suggests healthy demand. For example: a company’s sales have grown 14% a year for ten years.

EV/EBITDA. EV/EBITDA compares the whole value of a business (market value plus net debt) with its operating earnings before interest, tax and depreciation. It lets you compare companies with different debt levels. For example: an analyst compares two firms of the same size but with very different borrowings using one common multiple.

Current ratio. The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. It shows whether a company can meet its short-term obligations. For example: a company’s cash, stock and receivables are 1.8 times what it owes in the next twelve months.

client.quote: “How do I avoid a company whose profits look too good to be true?”

talk: “Check whether profits turn into cash over several years, whether growth is steady rather than a one-year spike, and whether the numbers are consistent across the statements. Surprises in those areas are a red flag.”
remember: Free cash flow is the real surplus.

title: What a futures contract is
concept: Futures are standardised contracts traded on an exchange. Learn the basic parts before touching one.

Derivative. A derivative is a financial contract whose value comes from an underlying asset such as a share, an index or a commodity. For example: a contract’s price moves because the Nifty moves, though no index units are owned.

Futures contract. A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an underlying asset at a fixed price on a set future date. It is standardised and traded on an exchange. For example: two parties agree today to trade an index at a fixed price one month from now.

Lot size. Lot size is the fixed quantity of the underlying in one futures contract, set by the exchange. You cannot trade less than one lot. For example: a contract is for 75 units of the underlying and cannot be bought in smaller pieces.
Expiry. Expiry is the date on which a futures contract ends and is settled. After it, the contract no longer exists. For example: a monthly contract reaches its last trading day and is closed out.

title: Margin and leverage
concept: Futures need only a fraction of the contract value as a deposit. That fraction is leverage.

Margin. Margin is the deposit you must keep with the broker to hold a futures position. It protects the exchange against defaults. For example: a trader puts ₹1 lakh aside to hold a contract worth ₹10 lakh.

Leverage. Leverage means controlling a large position with a small deposit. It magnifies both profits and losses relative to the money you put in. For example: a 2% move in the underlying changes the trader’s deposit by 20%.

Mark-to-market. Mark-to-market settles gains and losses every day: your account is credited or debited based on that day’s closing price. For example: at day end a trader’s account is debited ₹8,000 because the price fell.

Margin call. A margin call is a demand from the broker to add funds when losses reduce your deposit below the required level. For example: after three losing days, the broker asks a trader to deposit more money immediately.

client.quote: “I only need ₹1 lakh to trade a ₹10 lakh contract. That’s great, no?”
client.context: A client attracted by the small deposit.

talk: “The ₹1 lakh is a deposit, not your limit. If the contract moves 10% against you, you lose ₹1 lakh. If it moves further, you owe more. Leverage multiplies both gains and losses.”
remember: Margin is a deposit, not the loss limit.

title: Going long, going short
concept: Futures let you profit from a rise or a fall, and let you hedge a portfolio.

Long position. A long position is buying a futures contract. It gains when the price of the underlying rises and loses when it falls. For example: a trader buys an index future expecting the market to rise.

Short position. A short position is selling a futures contract. It gains when the price falls and loses when it rises, with no upper limit to the loss. For example: a trader sells an index future expecting the market to fall.

Hedging. Hedging means taking an opposite position to reduce the risk of an existing one, such as selling index futures against a share portfolio. For example: an investor holding many shares sells index futures to cushion a possible market fall.

Open interest. Open interest is the total number of futures contracts still open and not yet settled. It shows how much money is committed to the market. For example: data shows 40 lakh contracts remain outstanding at the end of the day.

client.context: A client who wants to benefit from a decline.

talk: “Yes, by selling a future you profit if the price falls, but you lose if it rises, and losses can be large. It is a tool for experienced participants or for hedging, not a casual bet.”

title: Pricing and settlement
concept: Futures prices sit close to the spot price plus the cost of carrying money until expiry.
Spot price. The spot price is the current market price of the underlying for immediate delivery. For example: the Nifty stands at 24,000 right now, regardless of any contract.

Basis. Basis is the difference between the futures price and the spot price. It narrows and reaches zero at expiry. For example: an index future trades 60 points above the index and the gap shrinks every day.

Cost of carry. Cost of carry is the cost of holding the underlying until expiry, mainly funding cost less any dividends. It explains why futures trade above spot. For example: the fair price of a futures contract adds the interest on the money needed to hold the asset.

Cash settlement. In cash settlement, the contract ends with a payment of the price difference in cash, with no delivery of the underlying. Index futures settle this way. For example: at expiry an index trader receives or pays the difference in rupees and no shares move.

client.quote: “Why is the future higher than the spot price?”
client.context: A client who noticed the gap on screen.

talk: “The future includes the cost of funding the position until expiry, so it normally trades slightly above spot. That gap, the basis, shrinks to zero by expiry.”

qs.why: Correct: Cost of carry is the cost of holding the underlying until expiry, mainly funding cost less any dividends. It explains why futures trade above spot. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

title: Using futures wisely
concept: Futures reward discipline. Most losses come from size, not from being wrong about direction.

Position sizing. Position sizing means deciding how much money to put in a single trade so that a loss stays small relative to your total capital. For example: a trader risks no more than 1% of capital on any one contract.

Stop-loss. A stop-loss is a preset exit point that limits a loss if the price moves against you. It controls risk but does not guarantee the exit price. For example: a trader decides in advance to exit if the index falls 1% below the entry.

Rollover. Rollover means closing a near-expiry contract and opening the same position in the next expiry, to keep the exposure going. For example: before expiry, a hedger sells the month’s contract and buys next month’s to keep the cover.

Index futures. Index futures are futures on an index such as the Nifty. They are cash-settled and are often used to hedge a diversified portfolio. For example: a fund manager hedges a basket of shares with a single contract on the market index.

client.context: An over-eager client.

talk: “That is how people lose everything. SEBI’s studies found that most individual traders in futures and options lose money. If you trade at all, risk only money you can lose and always use a stop-loss.”
remember: Position size is the main risk control.

title: Calls, puts and premium
concept: An option gives the right, not the duty, to buy or sell at a set price. The price you pay for that right is the premium.

Call option. A call option gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying at a fixed price on or before expiry. For example: a trader pays a small fee for the right to buy a share at ₹500 later, whatever the market price.

Put option. A put option gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying at a fixed price on or before expiry. For example: an investor pays a fee for the right to sell a share at ₹400 even if the price falls lower.

Premium. The premium is the price the buyer pays the seller for an option. It is non-refundable and is the buyer’s maximum possible loss. For example: a buyer pays ₹30 per unit for the contract and can lose no more than that per unit.

Strike price. The strike price is the fixed price at which the option holder can buy or sell the underlying if the option is exercised. For example: an option contract fixes ₹24,500 as the price at which the index can be bought.

client.quote: “What exactly is a call option?”
client.context: A client who heard about options from a friend.

talk: “A call gives you the right to buy at a fixed price until expiry. You pay a premium up front. If the share does not rise enough, the premium is gone, but that is all you can lose as a buyer.”
remember: Call = right to buy; put = right to sell.

title: Moneyness and value
concept: An option’s price is intrinsic value plus time value. Moneyness tells you where the market is relative to the strike.

In-the-money (ITM). An option is in the money when exercising it would give a profit relative to the market price: a call with the share above the strike, or a put with it below. For example: a call has a strike of ₹400 while the share trades at ₹450.

At-the-money (ATM). An option is at the money when the strike price is equal or very close to the current price of the underlying. For example: a call has a strike of ₹500 and the share trades at ₹500.

Out-of-the-money (OTM). An option is out of the money when exercising it would give no gain at the current price. Its premium is all time value. For example: a call has a strike of ₹600 while the share trades at ₹500.

Intrinsic value. Intrinsic value is the amount by which an option is in the money, which is what it would be worth if exercised right now. For example: a call struck at ₹400 on a share trading at ₹450 has ₹50 of immediate value.

client.quote: “Why did my option lose value even though the share did not move?”
client.context: A client puzzled by a falling option price.

talk: “Part of an option’s price is time value, which shrinks every day as expiry nears. If the share does not move enough, time decay eats the premium.”
remember: Out-of-the-money options have no intrinsic value.

title: The Greeks, in plain words
concept: The Greeks measure how an option’s price reacts to changes in price, time and volatility.

Delta. Delta shows how much an option’s price is expected to change for a ₹1 change in the underlying. It also hints at the chance of finishing in the money. For example: an option’s price rises about ₹0.60 when the share rises ₹1.

Theta. Theta measures how much value an option loses each day as expiry approaches, all else equal. It works against the buyer and for the seller. For example: an option loses about ₹2 of value every day even when the price does not move.
Vega. Vega measures how much an option’s price changes when expected volatility changes by one percentage point. For example: option prices jump across the board when markets become more nervous.

Implied volatility. Implied volatility is the market’s expectation of how much the underlying will move, read from option prices. Higher implied volatility makes options more expensive. For example: before a major announcement, option prices rise even though the share price has not moved.

client.context: A client who sees Greeks on the trading screen.

talk: “Delta tells you how much the option moves for a ₹1 move in the share. Theta tells you how much value it loses every day. Vega shows sensitivity to volatility. They help you understand the risks, not predict the market.”

title: Buying and selling options
concept: Buyers and sellers face very different risks. Know which side you are on.

Option buyer. The option buyer pays the premium and gets the right to exercise. The most they can lose is the premium, while the gain can be large. For example: a trader pays ₹20 for a contract and can lose at most that ₹20 per unit.

Option writer. The option writer, or seller, collects the premium and takes on the obligation if the buyer exercises. Gains are limited to the premium, losses can be very large. For example: a trader receives ₹20 for taking on the obligation to deliver if the price shoots up.

Break-even point. The break-even point is the price at which the option buyer neither gains nor loses, after counting the premium paid. For example: a call is struck at ₹500 with a ₹20 premium, so the share must pass ₹520 for a profit.

European-style option. A European-style option can be exercised only at expiry. Index and stock options in India are of this kind. For example: a contract can be exercised only on its final day, not before.

client.quote: “Selling options looks like easy money. Premium every week!”
client.context: A client attracted by regular premium income.

talk: “Option sellers collect small premiums often, but a sudden move can cause a loss many times larger. Many experienced traders use limited-risk spreads for that reason. It is not easy money.”
remember: Buyer: limited loss, time works against them.
Seller: limited gain, potentially large loss.

title: Simple strategies and sober facts
concept: A few simple strategies protect or enhance a portfolio. Speculation is another matter.

Protective put. A protective put is buying a put option on shares you own, so that losses below the strike are limited. It works like insurance and costs the premium. For example: an investor holding shares buys a put to guard against a sharp fall.

Covered call. A covered call is selling a call option against shares you already own. It earns premium but caps your gain if the price rises sharply. For example: an investor sells a call on shares held, collecting a fee and agreeing to sell at a higher price.

Straddle. A straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike and expiry. It profits if the price moves a lot in either direction. For example: a trader expects a big move after results but is unsure of the direction.

Bull call spread. A bull call spread buys a call and sells a higher-strike call. It lowers the cost and caps both the profit and the loss. For example: a trader buys a call at ₹500 and sells one at ₹550 to cut the cost, accepting a capped gain.

title: Why hold gold
concept: Gold is a store of value that often behaves differently from shares and bonds.

Store of value. A store of value keeps its purchasing power over long periods. Gold has long served this role across cultures and eras. For example: a family keeps a part of its savings in an asset that has held its buying power for centuries.

Diversifier. A diversifier is an asset that does not move in step with the rest of a portfolio, so it can reduce overall swings. For example: when shares fall sharply, a client’s gold holding often falls much less or even rises.

Safe-haven demand. Safe-haven demand is investors moving into gold during uncertainty, war or financial stress, which can lift its price. For example: during a geopolitical shock, investors buy gold and its price rises.

Inflation hedge. An inflation hedge is an asset expected to hold its value as prices rise. Gold has helped over very long periods but not every year. For example: over decades, the rupee price of gold has kept pace with rising prices, though with ups and downs.

client.context: A client chasing a rally.

talk: “Gold is a useful diversifier, usually a modest slice of a portfolio, not the whole plan. It earns no income, so its long-run return depends on price alone, and it can fall for years too.”

title: What moves the gold price
concept: Gold’s price is set globally in dollars and reaches Indians through the exchange rate and local duties.

Real interest rate. The real interest rate is the interest rate minus inflation. Gold pays no interest, so higher real rates make it less attractive. For example: bond yields rise well above inflation and gold becomes less appealing to investors.

Central bank buying. Central banks buy gold to diversify their reserves. Heavy purchases add steady demand and can support the price. For example: several central banks add tonnes of gold to their reserves in a year.

Rupee-dollar effect. Gold is priced in dollars, so when the rupee weakens against the dollar, the rupee price of gold rises even if the dollar price is unchanged. For example: the global gold price is flat but the rupee falls, and Indian gold prices go up.

Import duty and GST. India adds import duty and a GST on gold, so the local price differs from the international price converted to rupees. For example: the price on a local jeweller’s board is higher than the converted global price.

title: Physical gold: jewellery, coins and bars
concept: Physical gold is familiar but carries purity, cost and storage issues.

Hallmark. A hallmark is the official mark showing the purity of gold jewellery, issued under the BIS scheme. It carries a unique HUID code. For example: a buyer checks that the jewellery bears the BIS stamp and a unique six-character code.

Carat purity. Carat measures gold purity. 24 carat is almost pure gold, while 22 carat is about 91.6% gold mixed with other metals for strength. For example: a jeweller offers a ring marked 22 out of 24 parts gold.

Making charges. Making charges are the fee a jeweller adds for crafting the jewellery. They are not recovered when you sell the gold. For example: the bill adds a percentage on top of the gold value for design and labour.

Buyback spread. The buyback spread is the gap between the price at which you buy gold and the lower price at which a dealer buys it back from you. For example: a buyer finds the jeweller will pay less for old gold than the original price.

title: Paper and digital gold
concept: Financial forms of gold remove storage worries and cut costs.

Gold ETF. A gold ETF is a fund that holds gold and trades on the stock exchange like a share. Its price tracks the market price of gold. For example: an investor buys units on the exchange through a demat account that follow the price of gold.

Gold fund of funds. A gold fund of funds invests in gold ETFs. You can buy it without a demat account, but there is an extra layer of cost. For example: an investor without a demat account buys a mutual fund that invests in gold ETFs.

Sovereign Gold Bond. A Sovereign Gold Bond is a government security priced in grams of gold. It paid fixed interest on top of gold’s price movement, with an eight-year term. For example: an investor holds a government-issued bond that moves with gold and also pays 2.5% interest a year.

Digital gold. Digital gold is gold bought online from a platform that holds the metal for you. It is not regulated by SEBI, so the seller’s credibility matters. For example: an app sells a customer ₹500 of gold stored by a private vault provider.

title: Gold in a portfolio
concept: How much gold, and when, matters more than which form.

Asset allocation. Asset allocation is the split of a portfolio among asset classes such as shares, bonds and gold, based on goals and risk tolerance. For example: an adviser sets 60% equity, 30% debt, 10% gold for a moderate-risk client.

Rebalancing. Rebalancing means bringing a portfolio back to its target mix, usually by selling what has grown and buying what has lagged. For example: gold rallies and rises from 10% to 16% of a portfolio, so some is sold to return to 10%.

Gold loan. A gold loan is a loan taken against pledged gold. The lender holds the gold until you repay, and it can be sold if you default. For example: a borrower pledges ornaments with a lender to get a short-term loan.

Gold monetisation. Gold monetisation means depositing idle gold with a bank to earn interest instead of keeping it in a locker. For example: a household places unused gold with a bank and earns interest on it.

title: What makes silver different
concept: Silver is both a precious metal and an industrial material.

Industrial demand. Industrial demand is silver used in making things such as solar panels, electronics and batteries. It makes up over half of total silver demand. For example: a surge in solar panel production increases the amount of silver factories need.

Precious metal. A precious metal is a rare metal valued for investment and ornament. Silver counts as one, alongside gold, platinum and palladium. For example: a coin made of a rare metal is kept as a store of value.

Volatility. Volatility is how widely a price swings. Silver’s price usually moves up and down much more sharply than gold’s. For example: in a year when gold gains 10%, silver rises 30% and then falls 20% within months.

Gold-silver ratio. The gold-silver ratio is how many ounces of silver equal one ounce of gold in price. Traders watch it to judge whether silver looks cheap or dear relative to gold. For example: an analyst notes that the gold price is now 85 times the silver price.

title: What moves silver
concept: Silver reacts to the economy, the dollar, interest rates and supply.

Economic cycle. The economic cycle is the pattern of expansion and slowdown. Silver tends to be demanded more when factories are busy. For example: silver prices soften when factories reduce output during a slowdown.

By-product supply. Most silver is mined as a by-product of copper, lead, zinc or gold, so miners do not raise silver output just because the price rises. For example: a miner producing copper cannot quickly increase silver output even when prices jump.

Green-energy demand. Green-energy demand is the silver used in solar cells and electric vehicles. It has been a growing source of demand. For example: a government plan to build large solar capacity raises expected silver consumption.

Recycling supply. Recycling supply is silver recovered from old jewellery, coins and electronics. It adds to supply, especially when prices are high. For example: high prices bring a wave of old silver items to scrap dealers.

title: Physical silver
concept: Buying physical silver is possible, but costs and purity need care.
999 purity. 999 purity, or 99.9% fine, is the standard for investment-grade silver bars and coins. For example: a buyer checks that the bar is stamped 999 before paying.

Silver hallmark. A silver hallmark is a quality mark that shows the purity of silver articles, so buyers can verify what they are paying for. For example: a buyer checks for a quality mark on silver jewellery to confirm its fineness.

Storage burden. Storage burden is the practical cost of keeping physical silver safe. For the same value, silver occupies far more space than gold. For example: a household holding silver worth ₹5 lakh needs a bulky, secure place to keep it.

Premium over spot. The premium over spot is the extra amount charged by a dealer above the market price of silver, covering making, handling and profit. For example: a dealer sells a coin at a few per cent above the market rate.

title: Silver ETFs and funds
concept: Regulated silver products make buying and selling easier and cheaper than physical silver.

Silver ETF. A silver ETF is an exchange-traded fund that holds silver and trades like a share. Its price tracks the market price of silver. For example: an investor buys units on the exchange whose value moves with the silver price.

Silver fund of funds. A silver fund of funds invests in silver ETFs and can be bought directly from the fund house without a demat account. For example: an investor starts a SIP in a mutual fund that buys silver ETFs.

Tracking error. Tracking error is the gap between a fund’s return and the return of what it tracks. A smaller gap means the fund follows the silver price more closely. For example: a silver ETF returns 14.2% while the silver price rose 15%.

Premium or discount to NAV. An ETF can trade slightly above or below the value of its holdings. The gap is the premium or discount to NAV. For example: an ETF’s market price is 2% higher than the value of the silver it holds.

title: Silver in a portfolio
concept: Silver can add diversification, but its swings call for small positions.

Satellite holding. A satellite holding is a small position around a core portfolio. Silver suits this role because of its higher risk. For example: a client keeps most money in diversified funds and a small slice in silver.

Staggered buying. Staggered buying means investing in parts over time instead of all at once, which reduces the risk of buying at a peak. For example: a client invests the silver allocation in six monthly instalments.
Drawdown. A drawdown is the fall from a peak to a later low. Silver has seen deep drawdowns, so investors need patience. For example: silver falls 30% from its high before recovering.

Emergency fund. An emergency fund is money kept safe and accessible for unexpected needs. It should never be invested in volatile assets like silver. For example: a client sets aside six months of expenses in a liquid account before investing.

title: What a PMS is
concept: A PMS is a customised portfolio run by a SEBI-registered portfolio manager for wealthier investors.

Portfolio Management Service. A PMS is a service where a SEBI-registered portfolio manager manages a client’s securities portfolio, usually for high-net-worth investors. For example: a wealthy client hires a registered firm to build and run a share portfolio in her name.

Minimum investment. SEBI sets the minimum investment in a PMS at ₹50 lakh per client. Accredited investors can go lower. For example: a client with ₹30 lakh is told he cannot open a regular PMS account.

Segregated account. In a PMS, each client’s securities are held in a separate account in their own name, instead of in a pooled fund. For example: a client logs in and sees the exact shares bought for her, in her own name.

Portfolio manager. A portfolio manager is a SEBI-registered entity that makes investment decisions on behalf of clients under a signed agreement. For example: a registered firm decides which shares to buy and sell for a client under a written contract.

title: Types of PMS
concept: How much say the manager has, and how the strategy is built, define the service.

Discretionary PMS. In a discretionary PMS, the manager takes investment decisions on the client’s behalf without asking for approval of each trade. For example: the manager buys and sells shares in the client’s account without calling her for each trade.

Non-discretionary PMS. In a non-discretionary PMS, the manager recommends and the client must approve each transaction before it is executed. For example: the manager calls the client for approval before every purchase.

Advisory PMS. In an advisory PMS, the manager only recommends investments. The client decides and places the orders. For example: a firm sends buy and sell ideas, and the client places the trades himself.

Investment approach. An investment approach is the style a PMS follows, such as multi cap, small cap, value or growth. It defines what the manager buys. For example: a PMS focuses on a concentrated set of small companies with strong growth.

title: Fees and charges
concept: PMS fees vary widely and can quietly reduce returns.
Management fee. A management fee is a fixed percentage of the portfolio charged each year regardless of performance. For example: a PMS charges 2% of the portfolio value every year.

Performance fee. A performance fee is a share of profits charged above an agreed return, aligning the manager’s earnings with the client’s gains. For example: a manager takes 20% of the gains beyond a set hurdle return.

Hurdle rate. A hurdle rate is the minimum return the portfolio must earn before the manager can charge a performance fee. For example: the manager earns a profit share only on returns above 10% a year.

High-water mark. A high-water mark means the manager charges a performance fee only on gains above the portfolio’s previous peak value, so losses must be recovered first. For example: after a fall, no profit share is charged until the portfolio goes above its earlier peak.

title: Tax and reporting
concept: Because you own the shares directly, taxation works differently from a mutual fund.

Capital gains statement. A capital gains statement is a report from the PMS listing all sales and the gains or losses on them, used to file income tax returns. For example: at year end the client receives a report summarising profit and loss on every sale.

Churn. Churn is how often the portfolio’s holdings are bought and sold. High churn raises costs and creates more taxable events. For example: a manager replaces half the portfolio in a year, generating many taxable sales.

TWRR. TWRR, or time-weighted rate of return, measures performance while ignoring the timing of investor deposits and withdrawals, so managers can be compared fairly. For example: a PMS reports one return figure that is not affected by when each client added money.

Custodian. A custodian is an independent institution that safekeeps the client’s securities and settles trades, separate from the portfolio manager. For example: the client’s shares are held by an independent firm, not by the manager.

title: Risks and due diligence
concept: A PMS can be concentrated and expensive. Check before committing.

Concentration risk. Concentration risk is the danger of holding few stocks, so that one bad outcome can hurt the whole portfolio severely. For example: a portfolio holds only 15 stocks and two of them fall by half.
Benchmark. A benchmark is an index used to judge whether a portfolio manager has done better or worse than the market. For example: a manager’s return is compared with the Nifty 500 over five years.

Track record. A track record is the history of a manager’s results over several years and market cycles. A long record says more than one strong year. For example: an investor checks returns over five years and during market falls.

Exit load. An exit load is a charge levied if the client withdraws within a stated period. Always read the terms before investing. For example: a PMS charges 2% if the client withdraws within the first year.

title: What an AIF is
concept: An AIF is a privately pooled investment fund regulated by SEBI, for sophisticated investors.

Alternative Investment Fund. An AIF is a privately pooled investment vehicle regulated by SEBI, collecting money from sophisticated investors to invest under a defined strategy. For example: a group of wealthy investors puts money in a private fund that invests in start-ups.

Minimum commitment. SEBI sets the minimum investment in an AIF at ₹1 crore per investor, with exceptions for certain managers’ employees. For example: a client with ₹60 lakh is told he cannot invest directly in an AIF.

Private placement. An AIF raises money by private placement, not through a public offer. It cannot advertise to the general public. For example: the fund invites selected investors using an information document, not a public advertisement.

Investor limit. An AIF scheme can have at most 1,000 investors. This is why it is a private rather than a public vehicle. For example: a scheme closes to new money after reaching its permitted number of investors.

client.context: A wealthy client who heard about AIFs.

talk: “No. An AIF is a private pool for investors who can accept higher risk and long lock-ins. The minimum is ₹1 crore, it can invest in unlisted and unusual assets, and you cannot exit whenever you like.”

title: The three categories
concept: SEBI divides AIFs into three categories by what they invest in and how much risk they take.

Category I AIF. Category I AIFs invest in start-ups, early-stage ventures, social ventures, SMEs and infrastructure that the government wants to encourage. For example: a fund backs young technology companies and small manufacturers.

Category II AIF. Category II AIFs include private equity and private debt funds. They do not use leverage except for day-to-day operational needs. For example: a fund buys stakes in unlisted mid-sized companies, with no borrowing for investments.

Category III AIF. Category III AIFs use diverse or complex strategies, including hedge-fund style trading and leverage. They can be open-ended or closed-ended. For example: a fund goes long and short in listed shares and uses derivatives.

Angel fund. An angel fund is a sub-category of Category I that pools money from angel investors to invest in start-ups at the earliest stage. For example: a group of individuals pools funds to back a seed-stage company.

title: How an AIF works
concept: Money is committed upfront but drawn down over time, and returned as investments are sold.

Capital call. A capital call, or drawdown, is a request from the fund to pay part of the money you committed, when it finds an investment. For example: an investor receives a notice to pay 25% of her ₹1 crore commitment within 10 days.

Closed-ended fund. A closed-ended fund has a fixed life, such as seven years, and investors cannot withdraw until it ends or units are sold. For example: an investor’s money is locked until the fund winds up after its set term.

Lock-in and tenure. The tenure is the life of the fund, during which money is locked in. SEBI requires a minimum tenure of three years for Category I and II funds. For example: a private equity fund sets a term of ten years with extensions.
Distribution. A distribution is a payment returned to investors when the fund sells an investment or earns income. For example: the fund sells a stake and pays investors their share of the proceeds.
