title: Fees, tax and structure
concept: Layers of fees and a special tax treatment make AIFs different from funds you know.

Carried interest. Carried interest, or carry, is the manager’s share of profits above the hurdle rate, often around 20%. For example: after investors get their preferred return, the manager takes a fifth of further profits.

Preferred return. A preferred return is the minimum annual return investors get first, before the manager earns carry. It is also called the hurdle. For example: the manager earns carry only after investors receive 10% a year.

Pass-through tax. For Category I and II AIFs, income is generally taxed in the investor’s hands rather than in the fund, subject to the rules of the Income Tax Act. For example: the fund does not pay tax on its gains; investors report their share.

Trust structure. Most AIFs are set up as trusts, managed by an investment manager who runs the fund on behalf of the investors. For example: the fund is a trust with a manager running investments for contributors.

title: Risks and diligence
concept: Illiquidity, valuation and manager skill decide outcomes.

Illiquidity. Illiquidity is the difficulty of selling an investment quickly without a loss. AIF units are hard to sell before the fund ends. For example: an investor needs cash urgently but cannot withdraw from a closed-ended fund.

Valuation risk. Valuation risk arises because unlisted assets have no daily market price, so their reported value is based on estimates and models. For example: a start-up’s value in the fund is based on a model, not a market price.

Manager selection. Manager selection means judging a fund manager’s experience, track record, team and process before investing, because results vary widely. For example: an investor compares the experience and record of three managers before choosing one.

Accredited investor. An accredited investor is a person or entity that meets income or net worth tests set by SEBI and may get relaxations in certain minimums. For example: a high-net-worth individual who meets the tests is allowed to invest smaller amounts in some schemes.

title: What a SIF is
concept: SIF is a regulated product from fund houses for investors who want more than a mutual fund and less than a PMS.

Specialised Investment Fund. A SIF is a SEBI-regulated product offered by mutual fund houses with greater investment flexibility than regular funds, for investors who can take on more risk. For example: a fund house offers a new product that can take short positions for investors with larger tickets.

SIF minimum threshold. A SIF requires a minimum investment of ₹10 lakh per investor, counted across all SIF strategies of that fund house. For example: a client with ₹4 lakh cannot start a SIF with that fund house.

Mutual fund framework. SIFs are run by mutual fund houses under SEBI’s rules, with disclosures, a riskometer and a trustee, unlike private AIFs. For example: investors in a SIF receive a standard factsheet and a riskometer from the fund house.

Positioning. A SIF is positioned between a mutual fund and a PMS or AIF: more flexible than the first, more regulated and accessible than the others. For example: an adviser explains that the product has features between a mutual fund and a private fund.

client.context: A client who has heard about the new category.

talk: “A SIF is run by a mutual fund house under SEBI’s special framework. It can use strategies that ordinary funds cannot, so it needs a ₹10 lakh minimum and an investor who can handle more risk.”

title: Strategies in a SIF
concept: SIF strategies often combine long and short positions.

Long-short strategy. A long-short strategy buys securities expected to rise and takes short positions in those expected to fall, aiming to gain in both directions. For example: a manager buys one bank’s shares and sells another bank’s futures, expecting the first to outperform.

Short exposure. Short exposure is a position that gains when prices fall, taken through derivatives. A SIF can use it for up to a limited share of its net assets. For example: the fund sells index futures worth 20% of its assets to profit if the market falls.

Equity long-short fund. An equity long-short fund takes long positions in shares and uses derivatives to take short exposure, targeting returns across market conditions. For example: a fund invests in listed companies and sells futures on the weakest ones.

Strategy naming. SIF strategies carry standardised names so that investors know what they are buying, such as equity long-short or debt long-short. For example: a product name tells the investor that the fund takes long and short positions in equity.

client.quote: “What does a long-short strategy actually do?”
client.context: A client curious about a SIF brochure.

talk: “The manager buys shares expected to do well and sells, through derivatives, those expected to do poorly. This can cushion falls or add return, but it can also lose on both sides if the calls go wrong.”
remember: Long-short uses both buying and selling.
Skill matters more than the label.

title: How SIFs differ
concept: Compare the product with mutual funds, PMS and AIFs before choosing.

NAV-based pricing. A SIF reports a net asset value per unit, like a mutual fund, and investors buy and sell units at that value. For example: an investor sees a unit price published for the fund each day it is open.

PMS comparison. A PMS needs ₹50 lakh and holds securities in the client’s own name, while a SIF pools money into a fund with units. For example: one option shows individual shares in the client’s own demat account, the other shows units of a pooled fund.

AIF comparison. An AIF needs ₹1 crore, is privately placed and usually has a long lock-in, while a SIF is run by a fund house under mutual fund rules. For example: one product is a private placement with a multi-year lock-in, while the other is a regulated fund with units.

Redemption terms. A SIF has its own redemption terms set in the offer document, including how often you can redeem and any exit load. For example: the scheme documents say units can be redeemed only on certain days, with a notice period.

client.context: A client weighing options.

talk: “A PMS needs ₹50 lakh and holds shares in your name. A SIF needs ₹10 lakh and works like a fund with daily NAV and mutual fund style disclosures. The structures, taxation and reporting differ, so compare costs and rules.”

title: Risks of a SIF
concept: More flexibility means more ways to lose money.

Derivative risk. Derivative risk is the added risk of leverage, margin and mispricing when a fund uses futures and options. For example: a fund’s losses grow quickly because of its derivative positions.

Manager skill dependence. Manager skill dependence means returns rely heavily on the manager’s ability to pick both winners and losers, so outcomes vary widely. For example: two funds with the same strategy name deliver very different results.

Hedge cost. Hedge cost is the expense of derivatives used to protect a portfolio. It can reduce returns when markets rise. For example: in a strong rally, the fund’s hedges lose money and the fund lags the market.

Riskometer. The riskometer is a SEBI-mandated visual showing a scheme’s risk level, from low to very high, which investors should read before investing. For example: a client checks the dial on the factsheet before investing.

talk: “It can help, but it is not a guarantee. A wrong short can lose money in a rising market, and derivatives add complexity. Read the risk factors and invest only an amount you can afford.”

title: Suitability and tax
concept: A SIF is for a specific investor, and rules may change.

Suitability. Suitability means matching a product to an investor’s goals, risk capacity and understanding, before recommending it. For example: an adviser declines to place an anxious, near-retirement client in a complex strategy.

Surplus capital. Surplus capital is money that is not needed for goals, emergencies or regular living costs, and so can bear higher risk. For example: a client invests only the portion left after the emergency fund and goals are funded.

Tax by asset mix. The tax treatment of a SIF depends on its asset mix and the holding period, so investors should check the latest rules before investing. For example: two SIF strategies, one equity-heavy and one debt-heavy, are taxed differently.

Disclosure. Disclosure is the information a fund must provide, such as the scheme document, strategy, risks and portfolio, so investors can decide. For example: an investor reads the scheme document before investing.

client.context: A client near retirement.

talk: “A SIF suits experienced investors with surplus money and a clear understanding of long-short strategies. Retirement savings usually need simpler products. Tax treatment also depends on the fund’s asset mix, so check the latest rules.”

title: How insurance works
concept: Insurance moves a large, unlikely loss from you to a pool of policyholders.

Risk transfer. Risk transfer is moving the financial burden of a loss to an insurer in exchange for a premium. Many people share the cost of the few who suffer a loss. For example: a family pays a small yearly amount so that a large, rare loss will be paid by the insurer.

Premium. The premium is the amount you pay the insurer, monthly or yearly, to keep the cover active. Missing it can lapse the policy. For example: a policyholder pays ₹12,000 a year to keep the cover running.

Sum assured. The sum assured is the amount the insurer pays if the insured event happens, such as death during the policy term. For example: a policy promises ₹1 crore to the family if the policyholder dies within the term.

IRDAI. IRDAI is the regulator of insurance in India. It licenses insurers, sets conduct rules and protects policyholders. For example: a policyholder’s complaint about an insurer escalates to the insurance regulator.

client.quote: “I am young and healthy. Why do I need life insurance?”
client.context: A client in his late twenties with a young family.

talk: “Insurance is not for you, it is for the people who depend on your income. If something happens to you, the cover replaces what you would have earned. The best time to buy is when you are young, healthy and the premium is low.”

title: Term insurance
concept: Term insurance is the purest form of life cover: protection only, at the lowest cost.

Term plan. A term plan pays the sum assured to the nominee if the policyholder dies during the term. If the person survives, nothing is paid. For example: a 30-year-old buys a ₹1 crore cover for 30 years at a low yearly cost.

Policy term. The policy term is the number of years the cover lasts. It should usually run until the person’s earning years end. For example: a policyholder chooses cover until age 60, when she plans to retire.

Return of premium plan. A return of premium plan refunds the premiums if the policyholder survives the term, but costs much more than a plain term plan. For example: a buyer pays a far higher premium in exchange for getting premiums back at the end.

Rider. A rider is an optional add-on to a policy, such as critical illness or accidental death cover, for an extra premium. For example: a buyer adds an option that pays if she is diagnosed with a serious illness.

client.context: A client puzzled that nothing is returned.

talk: “Nothing, and that is why it is cheap. Like car insurance, you pay for protection, not for a return. If you want savings, invest separately in funds. Mixing the two usually gives you poor cover and poor returns.”
remember: Riders add cost; choose what you need.

title: How much cover
concept: Cover should be based on need, not on what the premium feels like.

Income replacement. Income replacement is the idea of buying enough cover to replace the earner’s income for the family for the years it would be needed. For example: a policy is sized so the family can meet expenses for fifteen years without the earner.

Liability cover. Liability cover means making sure the sum assured can clear outstanding loans, so the family does not inherit the debt. For example: a buyer adds the outstanding home loan to the cover she needs.

Cover multiple. The cover multiple is a rule of thumb: buy cover of about ten to fifteen times annual income, then adjust for loans and savings. For example: a person earning ₹12 lakh a year considers a cover of around ₹1.2 crore to ₹1.8 crore.

Inflation erosion. Inflation erosion is the loss in value of a fixed sum over time. A sum that looks large today buys much less in twenty years. For example: a ₹50 lakh cover bought today buys far less in twenty years.

client.quote: “Is ₹25 lakh enough?”
client.context: A client with a home loan and two children.

talk: “Start with what your family would need: loans to repay, children’s education, and living expenses for years. A common rule of thumb is ten to fifteen times your annual income, adjusted for your loans and savings.”

title: Savings-linked policies
concept: Endowment and ULIP plans bundle insurance and investment. Understand the trade-off before buying.

Endowment plan. An endowment plan combines life cover with a savings component, paying a maturity amount if the policyholder survives the term. For example: a policy pays ₹10 lakh at the end of 20 years if you survive, or the cover if you do not.

ULIP. A unit-linked insurance plan combines life cover with investment in market-linked funds, with charges deducted from the premium and the fund. For example: a policy invests part of the premium in equity funds and part in life cover.

Surrender value. The surrender value is the amount you get if you stop a policy before it ends. It is often much lower than the premiums paid. For example: a policyholder stops a plan after four years and receives less than he paid.

Mis-selling. Mis-selling is selling a product by hiding costs or exaggerating benefits, for example promising investment returns from an insurance policy. For example: an agent tells a customer that a policy will double his money in five years.

talk: “Bundled plans usually give lower cover and lower returns than buying a term plan and investing the difference separately. They suit people who value forced saving, but compare the costs and the surrender terms first.”

title: Buying and claiming
concept: Honest disclosure and good paperwork make claims smooth.

Material disclosure. Material disclosure means telling the insurer every fact that could affect its decision to cover you, such as illness, smoking and other policies. For example: a buyer lists his medical history and smoking status honestly in the form.

Nominee. A nominee is the person you name to receive the claim amount if you die. Keep the nomination up to date after life events. For example: a policyholder names her spouse to receive the amount, and updates it after marriage.

Free-look period. The free-look period is a window after receiving a policy during which you can cancel it and get your premium back, less small deductions. For example: a buyer reads the policy documents at home and cancels within the allowed days.

Claim settlement ratio. The claim settlement ratio is the share of claims an insurer paid out of those it received. A higher figure suggests better claim-paying record. For example: an insurer’s published data shows it paid 98 of every 100 claims received.

title: Cover basics
concept: Health insurance pays for hospital costs up to a limit, in two ways.
Sum insured. The sum insured is the maximum amount the insurer will pay for claims in a policy year. For example: a plan covers up to ₹10 lakh of hospital costs in a year.
Premium. The health insurance premium is the price paid each year for the cover. It rises with age, sum insured and city. For example: a 45-year-old pays more for the same cover than a 25-year-old.

Cashless claim. In a cashless claim, the insurer settles the bill directly with a network hospital, and you pay only the non-covered amount. For example: a patient is admitted and the hospital bills the insurer, not the patient, for covered costs.

Reimbursement claim. In a reimbursement claim, you pay the hospital yourself and then submit the bills to the insurer for a refund. For example: a patient pays at a non-network hospital and later sends bills to the insurer.

client.quote: “What is the difference between cashless and reimbursement?”
client.context: A client buying their first plan.

talk: “In a cashless claim the insurer pays the network hospital directly and you pay only what is not covered. In a reimbursement claim you pay first and claim later. Cashless is more convenient, but you need to use a network hospital.”
remember: Sum insured is the yearly limit.

title: What reduces your payout
concept: Several features quietly reduce what the insurer pays. Know them before you buy.

Co-payment. Co-payment is a fixed share of every claim that you pay yourself, such as 20%, with the insurer paying the rest. For example: the insurer pays 80% of each bill and the patient pays the remaining 20%.
Deductible. A deductible is an amount of the claim you must bear before the insurer starts paying. For example: a policy starts paying only after the first ₹50,000 of a claim is borne by the patient.

Room rent limit. A room rent limit caps the daily room charge the policy allows. Choosing a costlier room can reduce other charges proportionately. For example: a policy allows ₹5,000 a day, the patient takes a ₹10,000 room, and other charges are cut by half.

Sub-limit. A sub-limit is a cap on the amount payable for a specific illness or treatment, lower than the overall sum insured. For example: a policy pays no more than ₹40,000 for cataract surgery, whatever the sum insured.

title: Waiting periods and exclusions
concept: Not everything is covered from day one, and some things never are.

Pre-existing disease. A pre-existing disease is an illness you already had before buying the policy. Cover for it begins only after a waiting period. For example: a buyer already treated for diabetes asks when it will be covered.

Waiting period. A waiting period is the time after buying a policy before certain claims are payable. It includes a short initial wait and longer ones for some conditions. For example: a claim for a planned procedure is rejected in the first month of the policy.

Exclusion. An exclusion is something the policy does not cover, such as cosmetic surgery or injuries from certain activities. For example: a claim for a cosmetic procedure is declined because it is on the not-covered list.

Moratorium period. The moratorium period is a continuous stretch of cover, currently five years, after which claims cannot be contested on non-disclosure except for proven fraud. For example: after five unbroken years of cover, the insurer cannot reject a claim for an old non-disclosure.

talk: “You must declare it. Pre-existing conditions are usually covered only after a waiting period, up to three years under current rules. Hiding it risks the claim. After five years of continuous cover, claims are generally protected from challenge, except fraud.”

title: Choosing a plan
concept: The right plan balances sum insured, family needs and cost.

Family floater. A family floater is one policy covering the whole family under a single shared sum insured, usually cheaper than separate policies. For example: a couple and two children share a ₹10 lakh cover under one policy.

Individual policy. An individual policy covers one person with their own sum insured, so claims by others do not use it up. For example: each parent holds their own policy so one person’s claim does not affect the other’s.

Super top-up. A super top-up pays once your claims in a year cross a chosen threshold, giving a high additional cover at a low premium. For example: a family adds a ₹50 lakh cover that starts paying after the first ₹10 lakh of claims.

Restoration benefit. A restoration benefit refills the sum insured after it is used up in a year, usually for a different illness. For example: after a large claim in the year, the full cover is made available again.

talk: “A floater is cheaper for a young family, but the sum is shared. Parents usually need their own policies, because they claim more and raise the premium. A super top-up can add a large cover on top at a low price.”

title: Keeping your cover healthy
concept: Rewards, portability and network size improve the plan over time.
No-claim bonus. A no-claim bonus raises your sum insured, or lowers the premium, for each claim-free year. For example: a policyholder’s cover grows by 10% each year she makes no claim.

Portability. Portability lets you move your policy to another insurer while keeping credit for waiting periods already served. For example: a policyholder switches insurers and continues without restarting the waiting periods.
Network hospital. A network hospital is one that has an agreement with the insurer for cashless treatment. For example: a patient chooses a hospital on the insurer’s list to avoid paying upfront.

Pre and post hospitalisation. Pre and post hospitalisation cover pays medical costs for a fixed number of days before admission and after discharge. For example: the policy pays for tests the week before admission and follow-up visits afterwards.

title: Know where your money goes
concept: You cannot improve what you do not measure.

Net worth. Net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe. Tracking it shows whether you are becoming wealthier over time. For example: a household adds up savings and property, subtracts its loans, and finds the result.

Savings rate. The savings rate is the share of your income that you save each month. A higher rate usually builds wealth faster than chasing returns. For example: a person earning ₹1 lakh saves ₹20,000 a month, a rate of 20%.
Fixed expense. A fixed expense is a cost that stays the same each month, such as rent or an EMI. It is hard to cut quickly. For example: a household pays the same ₹25,000 rent every month.

Variable expense. A variable expense changes from month to month, such as dining out or shopping. It is where most savings are found. For example: a household’s food-delivery bill is ₹3,000 one month and ₹8,000 the next.

client.quote: “I earn well but nothing is left at month-end. Where does it go?”

talk: “Track every expense for a month. Most people find spending they had not noticed, from subscriptions to small daily buys. Once you see it, you can choose what to keep.”

title: Budgeting methods
concept: The best budget is one you will actually follow.

50-30-20 rule. The 50-30-20 rule splits income into needs (50%), wants (30%) and savings or debt repayment (20%). It is a starting point, to be adapted. For example: a household divides take-home pay into half for essentials, a third for wants, and the rest for savings.

Zero-based budget. In a zero-based budget, every rupee of income is assigned a purpose, so that income minus planned spending and savings equals zero. For example: a person plans each rupee of salary to bills, savings, and fun before the month starts.

Pay yourself first. Paying yourself first means moving savings out as soon as income arrives, before spending on anything else. For example: on salary day, a standing instruction sends 20% to an investment before bills are paid.

Sinking fund. A sinking fund is money set aside regularly for a known future expense, such as insurance premiums or holidays, so it does not strain a month. For example: a family sets aside ₹4,000 a month for an annual premium due next year.

title: The emergency fund
concept: An emergency fund stops one bad month from becoming a debt crisis.

Emergency fund. An emergency fund is a reserve of three to six months of expenses, kept safe and accessible for job loss, medical bills or urgent repairs. For example: a household keeps six months of costs in a liquid account before investing.

Liquidity. Liquidity is how quickly and cheaply an asset can be turned into cash without losing value. Cash and savings are highly liquid. For example: a saver can withdraw from a savings account in minutes, but a property takes months to sell.

Lifestyle inflation. Lifestyle inflation is spending that rises with each increase in income, leaving savings unchanged. For example: after every raise, a person upgrades the car and phone and saves no more than before.

Needs versus wants. Needs are essentials such as housing, food and insurance, while wants are things that improve life but are not necessary. For example: a family keeps rent and groceries while reducing branded clothing spend.

client.context: A client who wants to put every rupee to work.

talk: “The emergency fund is not for returns. It is for stability. Six months of expenses in a savings account or liquid fund means a job loss or medical bill does not force you to sell investments at a bad time.”

title: Debt order
concept: High-interest debt costs more than most investments earn.

Debt avalanche. The debt avalanche method repays the debt with the highest interest rate first while paying minimums on others. It saves the most interest. For example: a borrower targets the 36% card balance before the 9% car loan.

Debt snowball. The debt snowball method repays the smallest balance first for quick wins, then rolls that payment to the next. It is motivating, though it may cost more interest. For example: a borrower clears a ₹10,000 balance first, then uses that payment on the next.

Minimum due trap. Paying only the minimum due on a credit card leaves the rest to attract high interest, so the debt lasts for years. For example: a cardholder pays 5% of the bill each month and keeps getting charged interest on the rest.

Interest versus return. If a loan costs more than your investments can reasonably earn, repaying the loan is the better use of money. For example: a person with a 24% card balance compares it with a hoped-for 12% fund return.

talk: “Clear the card first. It charges far more than any reliable investment returns. After the high-interest debt is gone, invest. If you cannot clear everything at once, use the avalanche or snowball method.”

title: Goals and habits
concept: Goals give saving a purpose; habits keep it going.
SMART goal. A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. It turns a wish into a plan. For example: a family sets ₹5 lakh for a car down payment in three years.

Automation. Automation means using standing instructions and auto-debits so that saving and bill payments happen without relying on willpower. For example: a monthly SIP is debited the day after salary arrives.

Inflation. Inflation is the general rise in prices over time, which reduces what a rupee can buy. Goals should be set in future prices. For example: a cost of ₹10 lakh today is ₹13 lakh in a few years.

Annual review. An annual review is a yearly check of goals, budget, insurance and investments, adjusting for changes in income and life. For example: a couple sits down once a year to update their budget and goals.

title: How a loan works
concept: Four numbers define every loan.
Principal. The principal is the original amount you borrow. Interest is calculated on the outstanding principal. For example: a borrower takes ₹50 lakh as a home loan.
Interest rate. The interest rate is the cost of borrowing, shown as a yearly percentage of the outstanding loan. For example: a bank charges 9% a year on the unpaid balance.

Tenure. Tenure is the length of time over which the loan is repaid. A longer tenure lowers the EMI but increases total interest. For example: a borrower stretches repayment from 15 to 25 years to reduce the monthly payment.

EMI. An EMI, or equated monthly instalment, is the fixed monthly payment that covers both interest and part of the principal. For example: a borrower pays the same ₹40,000 on the same date each month for twenty years.

title: Interest rate types
concept: Whether your rate moves can change what you pay.

Fixed rate. A fixed rate stays the same for an agreed period, so your EMI is predictable even if market rates move. For example: a borrower’s rate stays at 9.5% for the next three years whatever the market does.

Floating rate. A floating rate changes with an external benchmark, so your EMI or tenure can go up or down when market rates change. For example: a borrower’s loan rate falls after the central bank cuts its policy rate.

Repo-linked rate. A repo-linked lending rate is a floating rate tied to the RBI’s repo rate, so changes in the repo rate pass through to borrowers. For example: a home loan rate is set at the repo rate plus a fixed spread.

Amortisation. Amortisation is the gradual repayment of a loan through instalments. In early years most of each EMI goes to interest. For example: in the first year of a 20-year loan, most of the EMI goes to interest.

talk: “With a floating rate, your interest follows an external benchmark such as the repo rate. When it rises, the bank can raise the EMI or extend the tenure. A fixed rate does not move for the fixed period.”

title: Reducing the cost of a loan
concept: Small steps early save a great deal over the loan’s life.

Prepayment. Prepayment is paying part or all of a loan ahead of schedule. It reduces the outstanding principal and the interest you pay. For example: a borrower uses a bonus to reduce the balance by ₹3 lakh.

Balance transfer. A balance transfer moves your loan to another lender offering a lower rate, subject to fees and terms. For example: a borrower shifts a loan to a bank that charges a lower interest rate.
Processing fee. A processing fee is a one-time charge by the lender when sanctioning a loan, usually a percentage of the loan amount. For example: a bank charges 0.5% of the loan amount upfront.

Total cost of borrowing. The total cost of borrowing is all the interest and fees paid over the loan’s life, not just the EMI. It shows the real price of credit. For example: a buyer compares two offers by adding the interest and fees paid over twenty years.

title: Credit scores
concept: A credit score summarises how reliably you repay.

Credit score. A credit score is a three-digit number, typically 300 to 900, showing your creditworthiness. A higher score means lower risk to lenders. For example: a bank sees a 780 score on a loan applicant and offers a lower rate.

Credit utilisation. Credit utilisation is the share of your credit limit that you are using. Keeping it low, often below 30%, helps your score. For example: a cardholder with a ₹1 lakh limit carries a ₹20,000 balance.

Hard enquiry. A hard enquiry is a lender checking your credit report when you apply for credit. Several in a short time can lower your score. For example: a borrower applies to six lenders in a month and sees the score slip.

Credit report. A credit report is a detailed record of your loans, cards and payment history maintained by credit bureaus. You can get a free copy once a year. For example: a borrower downloads her yearly free report and finds a wrong entry to dispute.

title: Cards and borrowing smart

Revolving credit. Revolving credit is credit you can use, repay and use again up to a limit, such as a credit card. Unpaid balances attract interest. For example: a cardholder spends, repays part, and carries the rest forward each month.

Secured loan. A secured loan is backed by an asset, such as a house or gold, which the lender can claim if you do not repay. Rates are usually lower. For example: a home loan is backed by the house being purchased.

Unsecured loan. An unsecured loan has no collateral, such as a personal loan or card, so the lender charges a higher rate to cover the risk. For example: a personal loan is given on the basis of income alone.

FOIR. FOIR, or fixed obligations to income ratio, is the share of income used for fixed payments such as EMIs. Lenders usually prefer it to stay below about 40 to 50%. For example: a bank checks that a person’s total EMIs stay within a limit of their monthly income.

title: Who counts as an NRI
concept: Status is decided separately for foreign exchange law and for tax.

NRI. A non-resident Indian is an Indian citizen who lives outside India for work, business or other reasons that suggest a long stay abroad. For example: an engineer leaves India for a multi-year posting in Singapore.

FEMA. The Foreign Exchange Management Act governs foreign exchange transactions in India, including the accounts and investments NRIs may hold. For example: a rule on how an NRI may bring money into India comes from the foreign exchange law.

Residential status for tax. Tax residential status depends on days spent in India in a year and earlier years, and decides whether global income is taxed in India. For example: a person’s Indian tax treatment changes after she spends fewer days in India.

OCI. An Overseas Citizen of India is a person of Indian origin holding a foreign passport and a lifelong visa-like card. For most investment rules, OCIs are treated like NRIs. For example: a US citizen of Indian origin holds a card allowing lifelong travel to India.

title: NRE, NRO and FCNR accounts
concept: Choose the account by where the money comes from and where you want it to go.

NRE account. An NRE account is a rupee account for money earned abroad. Balances and interest are freely repatriable, and the interest is generally tax-free in India. For example: an NRI deposits her foreign salary in a rupee account that she can send back abroad easily.

NRO account. An NRO account is a rupee account for income earned in India, such as rent or dividends. Interest is taxable and repatriation is limited to set annual amounts. For example: an NRI’s rental income from a flat in India is credited to a rupee account with limits on sending it abroad.

FCNR(B) deposit. An FCNR(B) deposit is a fixed deposit in a foreign currency, so the investor is protected from exchange-rate changes against rupee. For example: an NRI places a deposit in US dollars with an Indian bank and avoids rupee risk.

Repatriation. Repatriation means sending money from India back to your country of residence. Rules differ by account and source of funds. For example: an NRI moves savings from an NRE account to her overseas bank.

title: Investing in India

title: Tax for NRIs
concept: Indian income is taxed in India; the tax at home may depend on a treaty.

DTAA. A double taxation avoidance agreement is a treaty between two countries that prevents the same income from being fully taxed in both. For example: an NRI claims credit in her country of residence for tax already paid in India.

Tax residency certificate. A tax residency certificate is issued by your country of residence to prove you are a tax resident there, often needed to claim treaty benefits. For example: an NRI shows the paper from her country’s tax office to claim a lower rate under the treaty.

Indian-source income. Indian-source income is income earned or arising in India, such as rent from property or interest on an NRO account, and is taxable in India. For example: an NRI’s rent from a flat in Pune is taxable in India.

title: Who is an NRI
concept: Two laws use the word NRI differently: FEMA for money rules and the Income Tax Act for tax.

NRI under FEMA. NRI under FEMA is a person of Indian origin or citizenship who lives outside India for work, business, study or another purpose of uncertain duration. For example: a software engineer from Pune who has moved to Dubai on a work visa for several years is treated as an NRI for banking and investing rules.

Residential status for tax. Residential status for tax is decided each year by counting days spent in India, and it decides whether global income is taxed in India. For example: a person who spends fewer days in India than the test requires is treated as a non-resident for that year.

OCI cardholder. An OCI cardholder is a foreign citizen of Indian origin who holds a lifelong Overseas Citizen of India card, and is treated like an NRI for many banking and investment rules. For example: a Canadian citizen born in India uses an OCI card to open an NRO account.

RNOR. RNOR, or resident but not ordinarily resident, is a tax status where mainly income from India, plus some foreign income linked to India, is taxed. For example: a person who returns to India after many years abroad may fall in this status for a few years.

title: What India taxes

Global income. Global income is income earned anywhere in the world, and residents are taxed on it in India. For example: a resident who earns rent from a flat abroad reports it in India.

India-sourced income. India-sourced income is income earned or received in India, such as rent, capital gains on Indian assets and NRO interest, and it is taxable for non-residents. For example: an NRI who sells Indian shares pays Indian tax on the gain.

NRE interest exemption. NRE interest exemption means interest on an NRE account is generally free of Indian tax while the holder remains a non-resident. For example: an NRI earns interest on an NRE fixed deposit and pays no Indian tax on it.
TDS on NRI income. TDS on NRI income is tax deducted at source on payments to NRIs, often at higher rates than for residents. For example: a buyer deducts tax at source when paying an NRI for a flat.

title: Treaties and double tax
concept: Income can be taxed in two countries. Treaties and credits reduce the double bite.

DTAA. DTAA is a double taxation avoidance agreement between two countries that decides who may tax which income and at what rate. For example: an NRI in a treaty country claims a lower tax rate on Indian interest.

Tax residency certificate. A tax residency certificate is a document from the tax authority of your country of residence proving you live there for tax, often needed to claim treaty benefits. For example: an NRI shares this certificate with an Indian bank to get treaty rates applied.

Foreign tax credit. Foreign tax credit lets you reduce tax in one country by the tax already paid on the same income in another. For example: an NRI pays tax in India on rent and claims credit for it when filing in the country of residence.

Tie-breaker rule. A tie-breaker rule is a treaty test, such as permanent home or centre of vital interests, that decides which country treats you as resident when both claim you. For example: a person with homes in two countries uses this test to settle where they are resident.

PAN. PAN is the permanent account number needed for most financial transactions and tax filing in India. For example: an NRI gets a ten-character tax number from the income tax department before investing in mutual funds.

title: Capital gains basics
concept: A capital gain is the profit on selling an asset. Timing and type decide the tax.
Capital gain. A capital gain is the profit made when you sell an asset for more than its cost. For example: an investor sells shares for more than she paid.

Holding period. Holding period is the time between buying and selling an asset, which decides whether the gain is short term or long term. For example: units sold after a longer holding are treated differently from units sold quickly.

Cost of acquisition. Cost of acquisition is the price you paid for the asset, plus certain costs, used to work out the gain. For example: the purchase price of a fund unit is subtracted from the sale value.
Realised gain. A realised gain is a profit locked in by selling, and only such profits are taxed. For example: a rise in portfolio value is not taxed until units are sold.

Dividend taxation. Dividend taxation means dividends are added to your income and taxed at your slab rate. For example: a fund dividend raises the investor’s taxable income.

title: Losses and advance tax
concept: Losses can reduce tax if you use them properly.
Set-off. Set-off is adjusting a loss against a gain of the same or allowed type in the same year. For example: a loss on one share reduces the gain on another.

Carry forward. Carry forward is moving an unused loss to later years to offset future gains, usually only if the return was filed on time. For example: a loss this year is used against next year’s gain.

Tax-loss harvesting. Tax-loss harvesting is selling an investment at a loss to offset gains, done carefully and without losing sight of the investing plan. For example: an investor books a loss on a fund to reduce tax on a profit.
Advance tax. Advance tax is tax paid in instalments during the year when the liability is above a threshold. For example: a person with large capital gains pays tax before year end.

title: Regimes and filing

title: The retirement goal

Longevity risk. Longevity risk is the chance of outliving your savings. For example: a retiree lives longer than the plan expected.

Withdrawal rate. A withdrawal rate is the percentage of your savings you draw each year, a rule of thumb and not a guarantee. For example: a retiree draws a modest share of the corpus each year to make it last.

title: EPF and PPF
concept: Two long-term savings routes backed by rules and the government.

EPF. EPF is the employees’ provident fund, where employee and employer contribute a share of salary towards retirement. For example: a salaried person sees a monthly contribution to the provident fund in the payslip.

VPF. VPF is voluntary provident fund, where an employee adds extra contribution to the provident fund beyond the required share. For example: an employee chooses to put more of the salary into the fund.

PPF. PPF is the public provident fund, a government-backed long-term savings account with a rate set periodically. For example: a self-employed person opens a government-backed 15-year savings account for steady savings.
PPF maturity. PPF maturity is the 15-year term after which the account matures, with options to extend. For example: an investor’s PPF account matures after fifteen years.

title: NPS
concept: NPS is a pension scheme that you build until retirement and convert partly into a pension.

Age-based allocation. Age-based allocation is shifting from growth assets towards safer assets as retirement nears. For example: a saver reduces equity share in the last years.

No-claim bonus. A no-claim bonus is a discount on premium for each claim-free year. For example: a driver with no claims gets a lower premium at renewal.

concept: Many frauds happen through your phone.

OTP sharing. OTP sharing is giving the one-time password to someone else, which lets them complete a transaction in your name. For example: a caller pretending to be a bank officer asks for the code.

Remote access app. A remote access app is a screen-sharing tool a fraudster asks you to install so they can see and control your phone. For example: a fake support agent asks you to install a tool to fix a problem.

title: Investment scams
concept: Some scams look like opportunities.
Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi scheme pays earlier investors using money from new investors, and collapses when new money stops. For example: a scheme pays high returns to early members using fresh deposits.
Pump and dump. A pump and dump is when a group hypes a stock to raise its price and then sells to those who follow. For example: a group urges members to buy a thinly traded stock before selling.
Fake trading app. A fake trading app shows made-up profits to persuade you to deposit more, but you cannot withdraw. For example: an app displays growing profit, then blocks the withdrawal.

Impersonation call. An impersonation call is a call from someone pretending to be an official who threatens you and demands money. For example: a caller claims to be an officer and demands payment to avoid arrest.

title: Verify before you trust
concept: A quick check beats a long regret.

Registration check. A registration check is searching the regulator’s official list to confirm that an adviser, broker or fund is registered. For example: a person looks up an adviser on the SEBI website before paying.

Two-factor sign-in. Two-factor sign-in is an extra step, such as a code, that protects an account even if the password leaks. For example: a user switches on a second step for the broker login.

Call-back verification. Call-back verification is hanging up and calling the official number yourself to confirm a request. For example: a person calls the bank’s printed number after a suspicious call.

title: If it happens
concept: Speed matters. Quick action can stop money from leaving.

title: Why plan
concept: Without a plan, the law decides who gets what and how fast.

Estate. An estate is everything a person owns at death, such as property, savings, investments and belongings. For example: a person’s house, accounts and shares together make up everything they leave behind.

Intestate succession. Intestate succession is how assets pass under personal law when a person dies without a valid will. For example: a man dies without a will and his heirs inherit by the rules that apply to his religion.
Legal heir. A legal heir is a person entitled by law or a will to inherit from the deceased. For example: a spouse and children are among those entitled by law to inherit.

Succession certificate. A succession certificate is a court document that confirms who can claim certain assets such as bank balances and securities of the deceased. For example: a family obtains it to claim an account when there is no will.

title: Wills
concept: A will is the main tool to state who receives what.

Executor. An executor is the person named in a will to carry out its instructions. For example: a trusted friend is named to manage the distribution.

Witnesses. Witnesses are people who watch the maker sign a will and sign it themselves, and the law requires at least two. For example: two adults watch the maker sign and then sign the document themselves.
Codicil. A codicil is a document that changes or adds to an existing will. For example: a person adds a new bank account to the existing document through a short supplement.

title: Nomination and joint holding
concept: Nominations help move assets, but they do not always decide ownership.

Nominee. A nominee is a person named to receive an asset on the holder’s death, but the nominee is not always its final owner, as the will or law can decide. For example: a bank pays a deposit to the person named on the account, who then holds it for the heirs as the law requires.
Joint holder. A joint holder is a person who shares an account or asset with another, and in some modes the survivor continues to hold it. For example: a couple holds a demat account jointly.
Transmission. Transmission is the process of moving assets to heirs or nominees after the holder’s death. For example: a fund house transfers units to the legal heir after documents are submitted.
Mode of holding. Mode of holding is how joint accounts are operated, such as either or survivor or anyone or survivor. For example: a couple chooses either or survivor for convenience.

Family trust. A family trust is an arrangement in which trustees hold assets for the benefit of named beneficiaries as set out in the deed. For example: parents place assets in a trust for their children.
Gift deed. A gift deed is a document that transfers an asset to another person without payment. For example: a parent gifts a flat to a child by a registered deed.

Family settlement. A family settlement is an agreement among family members that settles how property is shared and avoids disputes. For example: siblings sign an agreement on the division of an ancestral house.

title: Bond basics
concept: A bond is a loan you give to a borrower in return for interest.

Bond. A bond is a loan an investor gives to a government or company, which promises interest and the return of the principal. For example: an investor lends money to a company and receives interest and the principal back later.
Coupon. A coupon is the regular interest a bond pays, usually stated as a percentage of face value. For example: a security pays a fixed interest percentage every year.
Face value. Face value is the amount printed on a bond that is repaid at maturity. For example: a security printed at one lakh repays that amount at the end.
Maturity. Maturity is the date on which the bond’s principal is repaid. For example: a bond matures after ten years and returns the principal.

title: Yield, price and rates
concept: Bond prices move in the opposite direction to interest rates.

Yield to maturity. Yield to maturity is the annual return you earn if you buy a bond at its current price and hold it to maturity. For example: a bond bought below face value has a higher yield than its coupon.
Interest rate risk. Interest rate risk is the chance that rising rates push bond prices down. For example: prices of existing bonds fall when new bonds pay more interest.

Duration. Duration measures how sensitive a bond’s price is to changes in interest rates, where a higher figure means more sensitivity. For example: a long-term bond falls more than a short-term bond when rates rise.
Reinvestment risk. Reinvestment risk is the chance that interest received must be reinvested at lower rates. For example: a coupon is reinvested at a lower rate than before.

Corporate bond. A corporate bond is a bond issued by a company, which usually pays more than a government bond because of added risk. For example: a firm raises money by selling bonds to investors.
Liquidity risk. Liquidity risk is the difficulty of selling an investment quickly at a fair price. For example: an investor cannot find a buyer for a little-traded bond.

title: Deposits, debentures and ladders
concept: Several fixed income choices sit next to bonds.

NCD. An NCD is a non-convertible debenture, a company bond that cannot be converted into shares. For example: a finance company raises funds by selling debt that cannot be turned into shares.
Floating rate bond. A floating rate bond is a bond whose interest resets with a benchmark rate. For example: a bond’s coupon rises when the benchmark rate rises.
Bond laddering. Bond laddering is buying bonds with different maturities so that money comes back at regular intervals. For example: an investor holds bonds maturing in one, three and five years.

title: IPO basics
concept: An IPO is the first time a company sells shares to the public.

IPO. An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a company sells its shares to the public for the first time and gets listed on an exchange. For example: a growing company raises money and lists on the stock exchange.
Primary market. The primary market is where new shares are issued and sold by the company, as in an IPO. For example: an investor buys shares directly from the issuer during the offer.

Secondary market. The secondary market is the exchange where existing shares are bought and sold among investors after listing. For example: an investor sells her shares on the exchange to another investor.
Offer document. An offer document is the prospectus that describes the company, its business, risks and use of funds. For example: an investor reads the risk section before applying.

client.quote: “Everyone is applying for this IPO. Should I?”
client.context: A client following the crowd.

talk: “Read the offer document first. Check the business, the risks and the price. Do not apply only because others are.”
remember: IPO is the first public sale.

title: Price and application
concept: The price comes from a band and bids, and the application uses your bank account.
Price band. A price band is the range in which investors can bid for shares in the IPO. For example: the issue states a lower and an upper price for bids.
Book building. Book building is the process of collecting bids within the price band to discover the final issue price. For example: demand from bidders helps set the final price.

Cut-off price. Cut-off price is an option where a retail investor agrees to buy at whatever final price is set within the band. For example: an investor chooses cut-off so the bid is valid at the final price.
ASBA with UPI. ASBA with UPI is a way to apply where the amount is blocked in your bank account and debited only if shares are allotted. For example: an applicant approves a mandate in a UPI app.

client.quote: “Will my money leave my account when I apply?”
client.context: A first-time applicant.

talk: “Your money is blocked, not taken. If shares are not allotted, the block is released.”

title: Allotment and listing
concept: Demand decides how many applicants receive shares.
Oversubscription. Oversubscription is when investors bid for more shares than are on offer. For example: an issue is subscribed many times its size.
Allotment. Allotment is the process of giving shares to applicants, which can be by lottery for retail investors when the issue is oversubscribed. For example: only some applicants receive shares.
Listing gain. A listing gain is the difference between the listing price and the issue price, which can also be a loss. For example: shares list above the issue price on the first day.

Investor categories. Investor categories are the groups in an IPO, such as retail, non-institutional and qualified institutional buyers, each with a share of the issue. For example: retail applicants bid within the retail limit.

client.quote: “I applied but got nothing. Did I do something wrong?”
client.context: A client with no allotment.

talk: “When an IPO is oversubscribed, allotment for retail applicants is often by lottery. Not getting shares is common and nothing you did wrong.”
remember: Listing can be a gain or a loss.

title: Judging an IPO
concept: A few checks beat the headlines.
Fresh issue. A fresh issue is when the company issues new shares and the money goes to the company. For example: a company sells new shares to fund expansion.
Offer for sale. An offer for sale is when existing shareholders sell their shares and the money goes to them, not the company. For example: an early investor sells part of the holding in the IPO.
Use of proceeds. Use of proceeds is the stated plan for how the company will spend the money it raises. For example: the offer document says funds will repay debt and build a plant.
Valuation. Valuation is the price of the company compared with its earnings, assets or similar companies. For example: an investor compares the price with listed peers before applying.

client.quote: “How do I know if the price is fair?”
client.context: A client comparing IPOs.

talk: “Look at where the money goes, who is selling and how the price compares with similar listed companies. Cheap or expensive is relative to what you get.”

title: Risks and cautions
concept: IPOs carry risks beyond market moves.
Grey market premium. Grey market premium is an unofficial, unregulated price signal for an IPO before listing, and it is not reliable. For example: a rumour says an IPO will list at a big premium.
Lock-in. A lock-in is a period during which certain shareholders cannot sell their shares after the IPO. For example: pre-IPO investors cannot sell for a set time.
SME IPO. An SME IPO is an issue by a small company on a separate platform, usually with higher risk and larger minimum investment. For example: a small company lists on the SME segment.
Anchor investor. An anchor investor is a large institution that agrees to buy shares before the IPO opens to the public. For example: institutions commit funds a day before the issue.

client.quote: “The grey market says it will list at double.”
client.context: A client excited by a tip.

talk: “The grey market is unofficial and can be wrong. Treat it as noise and decide on the business and price.”
